#4267. After 15 years, The Sims' best spin-off finally gets its due follow-up in The Sims 4: Royalty & Legacy

The Sims Medieval had a short but powerful run back in 2011, and now many of its best features are finally coming to the main franchise.

The Sims 4 developers recently promised an exciting year for the game, and the franchise as a whole, and we just got an early look at one of those first events. After some light teasing, the developer unveiled Royalty & Legacy, the game’s next expansion.

Royalty & Legacy’s first trailer debuted on Thursday, revealing a February 12 release date, and showing off the expansion for the first time.

There’s a lot going on in Royalty & Legacy, which is priced $40. For one, it introduces a new world, Ondarion, which is going to be the setting for your kingdom, as you join a race for the throne. The expansion introduces Dynasty and Nobility - two new systems you can use to create your own world of royal shenanigans.

Ondarion is made up of three neighborhoods (regions). Each region has a unique theme and culture, and they’re each ruled by a Dynasty. Dambele is a place that prioritises art and community. Verdemar is a chaotic world of outlaws and nobles. Finally, Bellacorde is an extravagant region known for opulence and romance.

Speaking of building places, Royalty & Legacy also adds a new Lot type, The Backroom Lot. It serves two functions that change with the time of day. For instance, it can be a library or gym in the morning, and shift into a night club at night. Dambele has its own library-turned-rave, for instance.

At the heart of Ondarion are all the possible fantasy lives and stories you can live. The Sims calls them Powershifts, and they include some well-known Arthurian fantasies and other, more silly ones.

Swordsmanship is the new 10-level skill arriving with the expansion, which further plays into those fantasies by letting your Sims duel. There are even Swordsmanship Tournaments you can watch take place across every neighborhood in Ondarion.

Then there are Secret Passageways, which let you speed up moving across the new regions. They essentially let your Sims teleport between designated passageways, either on their own lots, or other lots in the world. Some of these are hidden for you to find, while others you can create.

In terms of new careers, there’s the Noble Career, where your Sim can rise through several Noble Rankings by doing basically what nobles had to do in the middle ages to earn favour.

The aforementioned Dynasty System is how you can join any of Ondarion’s existing families, or start your own. You actually have a lot of say in what goes on, including the usual business of appointing heirs.

Of course, no royal roleplay would be complete without scandals, which is where the Scandals System comes in. Through it, you can create stories to discredit others, or even topple an entire dynasty.

In November, you may recall The Sims 4 introducing new free items inspired by West African culture. In creating that content, EA worked with a group of Simmers who have direct ties to West African countries.

The group’s guidance was once again utilised to build the Dambele neighborhood in this expansion, and some of the lots around the world of Ondarion were even created by members of the group.

While you wait for Royalty & Legacy to actually arrive, there’s more in The Sims 4 you can jump in right now. The game recently kicked off a collaboration with fashion brand Coach that brought several free items to Create a Sim, and Build Buy. That arrived alongside a free update, which already makes for a busy start of the year for The Sims 4.

#4265. A tiny injectable sensor could change how millions of people monitor blood sugar

Continuous glucose monitors help millions of people with diabetes keep track of their glucose levels in real time, making it easier to manage medications, dietary choices, and everyday activities. However, the high cost of these devices prevents some patients from accessing the technology.

Scientists at Texas A&M University have identified a potential way to make future glucose monitors more affordable. In a study published in ACS Measurement Science AU, the researchers found that a key sensing material for an experimental injectable glucose sensor performed just as well as a commonly used alternative at approximately one-tenth of the cost.

Many existing glucose monitoring technologies depend on enzymes to detect glucose. The Texas A&M team is pursuing a different approach that uses fluorescent molecules and near-infrared light. By measuring variations in the fluorescent signal, researchers can determine changes in glucose concentration without relying on enzymes.

The technology relies on a process called competitive binding. Within the sensor, glucose and a fluorescent sugar compound compete to occupy binding sites on a protein called concanavalin A, or ConA. As glucose levels rise, this competition alters the fluorescent signal, providing a way to measure glucose concentration.

After evaluating several compounds that bind to the protein, the team identified β-mannopentaose as a promising alternative to α-mannopentaose, a more expensive compound used in previous versions of the sensor. Despite its substantially lower price, β-mannopentaose delivered comparable sensing performance. It also produced promising results in artificial interstitial fluid, a laboratory solution that recreates conditions beneath the skin.

"The surprising part was how closely the lower-cost material matched the performance of the more expensive alternative," said Dr. Sayantan Tripathy, assistant research scientist in Texas A&M's Optical and Bio-Sensing Laboratory and the study's lead author. "In this case, the cheaper option wasn't really a compromise, and that's an important finding when you're thinking about future glucose-monitoring technologies."

"Developing an affordable glucose sensor means considering the cost of the individual materials as well as how well they work together," said Dr. Gérard L. Coté, principal investigator of the study and a professor of biomedical engineering in the College of Engineering. "This study shows that we can substantially reduce the cost of one sensing component while maintaining comparable performance, giving us a promising foundation for further development."

A Tiny Injectable Sensor Beneath the Skin

To create an injectable sensor, the researchers embedded the glucose detection materials within a small hydrogel designed to remain in the tissue beneath the skin. The gel holds the sensing materials in place while allowing glucose molecules to move through it, where their concentration can be measured.

During laboratory experiments, more than 94% of the sensing assay remained within the hydrogel after seven days. The results demonstrate that the less expensive sensing chemistry is compatible with an injectable glucose monitoring system.

"When new medical technologies are expensive, access can be limited," said Dr. Melissa Grunlan, study co-author, professor of biomedical engineering in the College of Engineering and professor of chemistry in the College of Arts and Sciences. "Our goal is to develop sensors that are not only effective but affordable for the people who rely on them."

Although the experimental sensor has shown encouraging results, it remains at the proof-of-concept stage. Further development and testing will be necessary before the technology can be considered for clinical use. Nevertheless, the findings indicate that reducing material costs does not necessarily require sacrificing sensing performance.

Making Diabetes Monitoring More Accessible

The research highlights the importance of factoring affordability into the design of new medical technologies from the outset. Finding ways to reduce manufacturing expenses while maintaining performance could eventually expand access to continuous glucose monitoring, particularly among patients who cannot currently afford advanced monitoring devices.

The researchers intend to further refine their technology and investigate other components that could enhance its performance, extend its useful lifespan, and make it more practical.

"While the work remains in the research stage, the findings suggest that future glucose-monitoring technologies may not have to rely on expensive materials to deliver effective results," Tripathy said.

"Our long-term goal is to develop a reliable, affordable injectable glucose sensor that can expand access to continuous glucose monitoring, particularly for people in under-resourced communities and those without adequate insurance coverage," Coté said. "Reducing the cost of the sensing materials is one step toward making these technologies accessible to more people who need them."

The research team consisted entirely of Texas A&M researchers. Alongside Tripathy, Coté, and Grunlan, the team included Dr. Carolina Martinez, Anthony Dongchau, and Samyucktha Ganesapandian. Funding was provided by the National Science Foundation (NSF) Engineering Research Center for Precise Advanced Technologies and Health Systems for Under-resourced Populations.

#4261. Breathing less oxygen tripled lifespan in mice with a deadly brain disorder

Oxygen is essential for human survival and for most forms of life. Yet under certain conditions, it can become dangerously toxic, causing serious damage to the body.

In the brain, excessive oxygen levels have been linked to a rare and often fatal childhood disorder called 3-MGA, as well as Leigh syndrome (the most common pediatric mitochondrial disease), Parkinson's disease, and premature aging. Researchers at Gladstone Institutes are now investigating a promising approach that could potentially help treat these conditions by reducing the amount of oxygen available to the body, a strategy known as hypoxia therapy.

For the past decade, Gladstone Investigator Isha Jain, PhD, has studied how oxygen levels influence health and disease. Her research has explored how the reduced oxygen availability at high altitudes can produce beneficial effects in conditions ranging from Leigh syndrome and diabetes to solid tumors.

Expanding the Potential of Hypoxia Therapy

Jain and her colleagues wanted to determine whether lowering oxygen levels could also benefit people with other rare and common conditions involving mitochondrial dysfunction and neurological damage.

For a new study published in Nature Metabolism, the team partnered with James Shorter, PhD, professor of biochemistry and biophysics at the University of Pennsylvania, and Daniel Southworth, PhD, professor of biochemistry and biophysics at UC San Francisco.

The researchers discovered that a malfunctioning protein known as HTRA2 can cause oxygen to accumulate to dangerous levels in tissues. Remarkably, reducing the oxygen concentration in the air dramatically extended lifespan and improved brain function in mice experiencing motor neuron degeneration caused by defective HTRA2.

"This protein is linked to many other conditions, so our findings suggest that hypoxia therapy could be transformative for treating many neurological diseases," says Jain, who is also a core investigator at Arc Institute.

How Excess Oxygen Becomes Toxic to the Brain

Most cells contain tiny structures called mitochondria, which use oxygen to generate the energy the body needs to function. One of the most important components of this energy production system is Complex 1, the largest molecular machine within the mitochondria's respiratory machinery.

"Every time we breathe, 90 percent of the oxygen we consume goes to our mitochondria," says Ankur Garg, PhD, postdoctoral fellow in Jain's lab and first author of the study. "But if Complex 1 malfunctions, the mitochondria can no longer burn off oxygen at normal rates."

When mitochondria lose their ability to consume oxygen efficiently, the unused oxygen can accumulate in surrounding tissues and eventually reach toxic levels. This process can contribute to the brain damage associated with certain mitochondrial and neurological disorders. The researchers suspected that reducing oxygen availability might help prevent some of this damage.

Identifying Genetic Causes of Oxygen Toxicity

To identify diseases that might respond to hypoxia therapy, the team revisited data from an earlier large experiment. They searched for genes whose absence impaired cell growth under normal oxygen conditions but allowed cells to grow normally when oxygen levels were reduced.

By comparing these results with a database of known genetic disorders, the researchers identified 75 genes directly associated with diseases that could potentially benefit from hypoxia therapy.

Among the most promising candidates was the gene encoding HTRA2. Further investigation revealed that HTRA2 works alongside another protein (CLPB) to maintain the structural integrity of Complex 1.

"Together, these two proteins act like a clean-up crew inside mitochondria, preventing the machinery from becoming clogged with clumps of misfolded proteins," says Jain.

The team found that when HTRA2 and CLPB are absent or malfunctioning, this cellular maintenance system breaks down. As a result, a critical component of Complex 1 stops functioning properly.

Breathing Less Oxygen Triples Lifespan in Mice

To determine whether reducing oxygen levels could provide therapeutic benefits in a living organism, the researchers conducted experiments on mice deficient in HTRA2.

Mice that breathed air containing less oxygen lived three times as long as those breathing normal atmospheric air, which contains approximately 21 percent oxygen. The treatment also reduced inflammation in the striatum, a region of the brain.

"By showing these mice could be successfully treated with low oxygen, our study expands the potential of hypoxia therapy to a wide range of conditions that affect mitochondrial Complex 1, either directly or indirectly as in the case of HTRA2 deficiency," Garg says. "This will motivate a broader application of 'turning the oxygen dial' to conditions ranging from rare genetic diseases to common neurological conditions and beyond."

Although the experiments involved having mice breathe air with reduced oxygen concentrations, Jain and her colleagues are working toward a more practical approach. They are developing a drug called HypoxyStat that could potentially reproduce the therapeutic benefits of low oxygen through a pill or injection.

"Right now, no treatments are uniformly available for mitochondrial diseases, and hypoxia therapy offers the hope that we could treat not just one, but many of these genetic conditions," Jain says. "We're working hard to make it a practical treatment for human patients in the clinic."

#4260. Halo: Campaign Evolved Gets Firefight Mode In Free Update This Winter

Halo: Campaign Evolved is getting the fan-favorite Firefight mode via a free update this winter, an Xbox Wire post announces. The update will allow players to team up in cooperative wave-based PvE.

Firefight, which debuted in Halo 3: ODST, lets up to four players team up to survive waves of enemies. The mode has become a popular staple and has appeared in multiple Halo games, but this will be the first time that it has been retroactively added to the original entry.

Xbox FanFest attendees, a global multi-city event, will be the first to go hands-on with Campaign Evolved’s take on Firefight. Additionally, more details about Firefight will be shared during Halo Fest in Seattle on December 12-13, where the mode will also be playable for attendees.

#4259. Tomorrow's Battlefield 6 patch somehow makes jets more useless, improves armor bar visibility in Redsec

The first Battlefield 6 patch of the year is almost here, bringing a smattering of changes, including one that doesn't quite make sense.

Battlefield 6’s promised, season-extending update has been officially detailed. The patch, version 1.1.3.5, arrives tomorrow, January 20 right when Season 1 was supposed to end. Part of the update’s goal is to extend the current season, until Season 2 kicks off in the middle of February.

Update 1.1.3.5 does, of course, have a change log of its own that goes beyond just the season’s extension, but the changes fall somewhere between not very exciting, and a bit puzzling.

Patch 1.1.3.5 is, for all intents and purposes, a smaller update. When Battlefield Studios announced it earlier last week, the developer didn’t promise any major changes or fixes, so expectations never got out of hand.

The patch is mainly made up of bug fixes, but it does have three key areas of improvements to gameplay. There’s a big focus on melee combat, how responsive/unresponsive it is with the various melee tools, and how melee behaviour interacts with sprinting and other animations.

The end result should be faster attack speeds for the knife, and clearer wind-up animations for both the knife and the sledgehammer. The timing dictating when melee damage gets credited has also been made more consistent in different environments.

Interestingly, sprint is now only interrupted when the melee attack reaches its target. As it stands, sprinting is only interrupted after the full duration of the animation has been completed, which adds to the that perceived feeling of sluggishness.

The other major, and arguably most confusing is the nerf to jet cannons. The patch is going to make jets far less stronger against other air vehicles, requiring 40% more hits to destroy a target. This is puzzling because jets - and air vehicles in general - are already the least survivable in Battlefield 6.

And, considering how the rest of a jet's arsenal is either situational or nearly ineffective, the cannons were really the one guaranteed way of downing other air vehicles, so long as you manage to land your shots consistently. While the change is wellmeaning, the percentage will likely be reduced in future patches.

Finally, the update makes a few refinements to UI across the game, though mainly aimed at Redsec and modes where players wear armor. Armor bar visibility has been improved, and there’s a fix for the annoying bug that sometimes caused the armor bar to disappear every few seconds.

Read on below for the 1.1.3.5 change log.

#4257. This dietary supplement may have an unexpected benefit for the brain

A dietary supplement known as urolithin A may help the brain meet its increased demand for oxygen and nutrients during mentally challenging activities. In a clinical trial led by researchers at the University of Oklahoma, middle-aged adults with obesity who took the supplement experienced increased blood flow to the brain while performing a memory task. The findings, published in JAMA Network Open, could shed new light on how urolithin A influences blood vessel function and brain health.

Obesity can affect how blood vessels function, potentially disrupting circulation throughout the body and brain. To investigate whether urolithin A could help counter these effects, the research team recruited 50 adults with obesity between the ages of 40 and 64 for a randomized clinical trial. For four weeks, participants took either 1,000 milligrams of urolithin A each day or a placebo.

Urolithin A Increases Blood Flow to the Brain

During a demanding memory exercise, participants who received urolithin A showed a greater increase in brain blood flow than those in the placebo group. The difference was especially noticeable in the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, an area that plays an important role in working memory, the ability to temporarily hold and process information.

However, the researchers observed no significant improvement in blood vessel function in the arm or in participants' performance on memory tests. According to the research team, this is the first study in humans to document an effect of urolithin A on the function of blood vessels in the brain.

"The brain needs an adequate supply of blood to meet the demands of mental activity," said the study's first author, Ana Clara da Costa Pinaffi Langley, Ph.D., an assistant professor in the Department of Nutritional Sciences at the OU College of Allied Health on the OU Harold Hamm Health Campus. "We found that urolithin A increased blood flow to the brain during a memory task, suggesting the supplement may help the brain meet its increased need for oxygen and nutrients when it is working harder. We plan to conduct more research to understand what this finding means for brain health."

A Natural Compound Produced by Gut Bacteria

The human body can produce urolithin A with the help of certain gut bacteria. These microorganisms generate the substance by breaking down naturally occurring compounds in foods such as pomegranates, strawberries, and walnuts.

Not everyone produces the same amount of urolithin A. Previous research suggests that the ability to generate the compound naturally tends to diminish as people grow older and their body mass index increases, Langley explained. Urolithin A can also be obtained directly through dietary supplements.

Participants tolerated the supplement well throughout the trial. However, the researchers cautioned that the study involved a relatively small number of people at a single research site. Larger, longer clinical trials will be necessary to better understand the supplement's effects.

Could Urolithin A Support Healthier Brain Aging?

Although the increase in brain blood flow is encouraging, it remains unclear whether this change could translate into lasting improvements in cognitive health.

"These findings offer an interesting starting point for understanding how urolithin A affects the brain," said study co-author Andriy Yabluchanskiy, M.D., Ph.D., an associate professor in the Department of Neurosurgery at the OU College of Medicine. "Although we saw increased blood flow to the brain during mental activity, participants did not demonstrate measurable improvements in memory or attention. Future studies will need to determine whether taking the supplement for a longer period leads to meaningful improvements in cognitive function or other health benefits."

For Langley, the broader aim is to extend healthspan, the portion of a person's life spent in good health.

"The idea is to mitigate cognitive decline," she said. "We want to expand the time that people are living healthier lives."

Materials provided by University of Oklahoma. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#4256. Fnatic confirms Razork exit as Lospa’s SK Gaming move deepens 2027 rebuild

Fnatic has confirmed the departure of its longest-serving player, jungler Razork, who is set to join Team Heretics. With support Lospa also set to leave, the London club faces a near-total LEC roster rebuild for 2027.

Fnatic has made its first confirmed exit official as it rebuilds its LEC roster for 2027. Razork was the London club’s longest-serving player and its main playmaker. He leaves after five seasons in the jungle.

The club marked the departure with a farewell video titled “Thank You, Iván”. In it, Fnatic recalls him arriving as a young player with huge ambition. He had entered the LEC with Misfits Gaming in 2020 before moving to Fnatic in 2022. The club later extended his contract to run through 2026.

His next stop appears to be Team Heretics. Sheep Esports reported that the 26-year-old will play alongside midlaner Jackies and support Jun. Heretics had already tried to sign him a year earlier. On that occasion it agreed a buyout with Fnatic but could not agree terms with the player.

The rebuild runs deeper than the jungle. Every Fnatic team member except Lospa was due out of contract in 2026. The support was signed until the end of 2027.

That deal will not keep him at Fnatic either. Lospa has reportedly agreed verbally to join SK Gaming for 2027. No buyout is involved in moving his contract between the two clubs. With that move, the one contract running beyond 2026 also leaves the club.

In the jungle, Yike is set to replace Razork in a 2027 line-up of Soboro, Yike, Vladi, Doggo and Labrov, according to Sheep Esports sources.

The overhaul follows a difficult year. Fnatic finished eighth in LEC 2026 Versus. It then placed seventh in Spring, which ended on 10 May. Summer brought the same finishing position.

A loss to GIANTX on 30 August kept the team out of the Summer playoffs. That defeat left the club absent from Worlds for the first time since 2016.

5 years of memories. it was an honour to see you grow into the person and player you are 🧡 https://t.co/F3TWY9WZqq pic.twitter.com/K3K3EQICZ1

For the UK scene, the scale of change matters. Fnatic is one of the LEC’s best-supported clubs among British fans.

The club has also opened a search for a League of Legends General Manager. Its job advert says Fnatic goes into a rebuild in 2027. The new hire will run recruitment of players, coaches and staff, including transfers and benchings, and will manage the team’s budget.

#4255. Heartopia surprise launches on Steam and shockingly, everyone seems to be happy

Heartopia players didn't actually end up having to wait too long to play the game on Steam, which is certainly not what anyone expected.

Heartopia has officially arrived on Steam, only a little over a week after it launched on iOS and Android. When the game’s release date was announced back in December, developer XD said it was pushing back the Steam release without offering any hints about how long the delay was going to be.

While the game can be played on PC through TapTap, the developer’s own emulator, many had been anticipating the Steam launch. So you can imagine that when the free-to-play life sim game surprisingly showed up on Valve’s platform on Saturday, there were a lot of happy people.

Heartopia’s Steam release has, much like mobile launch, been a success. We do know that the game reached the number one spot across app stores in over 50 countries, and though the Steam numbers may not be as record-breaking, everything is looking pretty good.

The game peaked at a decent 28,815 concurrent players (via SteamDB) on Steam one day after it launched, and considering how sticky it has been with the majority of those players so far - and the fact the launch itself was a surprise - there’s every chance those figures will improve over the course of this week as it picks up momentum.

Steam user reviews have similarly been quite positive, with the overall rating currently sitting at Mostly Positive, based on over 1,400 reviews.

You’re still need either a Google, Facebook, or Apple account to log into the game, same as you would on mobile. The Steam version does support cross-play with other platforms, so you’ll be able to play with your friends on mobile.

We’ve been playing a lot of Heartopia ourselves, and have been updating and expanding our guides. If you’re looking to get started, such as with how to add and play with friends, how to regain Energy, and how to unlock home plots, our guides offer the best place to start.

Once you’re past the initial hump, you’ll probably be looking for where to find things like mushrooms, bugs, fish, and birds, so definitely bookmark those, too. If you simply like free stuff, our Heartopia codes page is a must read before playing.

#4254. God Of War Sons Of Sparta Gets PS4 Version And New Content Next Monday

It's been about nine months since Sony Santa Monica and Mega Cat Studios dropped God of War Sons of Sparta as a surprise reveal and launch during a State of Play. If you haven't checked it out yet, the developers are giving you some new reasons to today, unveiling two new modes and a new platform: PlayStation 4.

If you don't remember, God of War Sons of Sparta is a prequel spin-off of the God of War series, showing protagonist Kratos as a 13-year-old soldier, long before his god-killing days. The game features 2D combat and a Metroidvania-style map, along with a fully voiced cast of characters including Scott Menville (who you might recognize as Robin in Teen Titans) as Kratos' brother Deimos, Jack Quaid (who will voice a different character in God of War Laufey next year), and TC Carson, who returns from the original trilogy as the voice of adult Kratos.

Announced in a post on the PlayStation Blog today, Sons of Sparta is making the jump back to Sony's previous console, which is now (brace yourself) 13 years old. Sons of Sparta's 2D pixel art is far less demanding than the other God of War entries, though, so it's no surprise this was possible – it's mainly surprising that they're doing it at all.

For PS5 players who already own the game, developer Mega Cat is also adding two new modes: Hermes Mode and Erebus Mode. Hermes Mode, named after the Greek god of wind, mail, and speed, is a speedrun mode that encourages you to beat the game as quickly as possible, complete with a split-based timer in the upper right-hand corner of the screen. Meanwhile, Erebus Mode, named after one of the domains of the underworld (you'll be familiar with it if you've played the Hades games), makes the game far deadlier as Kratos and all his foes die in a single hit. You'll have to wait until you beat the game once to unlock Erebus Mode, but you can access Hermes Mode from a fresh save by entering the following (and semi-familiar) code in the start menu: Up, Up, Down, Down, Left, Right, Left, Right, L1, R1, Touchpad.

The free update and PS4 version will be available next Monday, November 16, at midnight local time. For more Sons of Sparta, check out our review. For more God of War, bad news: God of War Laufey was just delayed until May.

#4253. Common supplements rival antibiotics in treating severe gum disease

A familiar dietary supplement combined with low-dose aspirin may offer an unexpected alternative to antibiotics for people with severe gum disease. In a year-long clinical trial, patients who received omega-3 and aspirin alongside conventional periodontal treatment experienced nearly identical clinical benefits to those who received antibiotics. Perhaps even more surprisingly, the improvements were still evident six months after supplementation ended.

The findings, published in the Journal of Periodontology, come from researchers affiliated with Albert Einstein Israelite Hospital, Guarulhos University (UNG), the University of Taubaté (UNITAU), and the Ribeirão Preto School of Dentistry at USP (FORP-USP) in Brazil, as well as Harvard University in the United States.

The study suggests that combining omega-3 with low-dose acetylsalicylic acid (ASA), better known as aspirin, could reduce the need for antibiotics in certain patients. The discovery is particularly timely given growing worldwide concerns about antibiotic resistance, which occurs when bacteria develop the ability to survive exposure to drugs designed to kill them.

Why Severe Gum Disease Is So Difficult To Treat

Researchers monitored 109 patients with advanced periodontitis over 12 months. Periodontitis is a chronic inflammatory disease that develops when bacteria accumulate below the gumline, triggering an immune response that can gradually damage the tissues and bone that hold teeth in place. Without proper treatment, the disease can cause teeth to loosen and eventually fall out.

As periodontitis progresses, spaces known as periodontal pockets form between the teeth and gums. These pockets can become increasingly deep, making it difficult to remove harmful bacteria through ordinary brushing and flossing.

"Patients with severe disease have very deep pockets, which act as reservoirs for bacteria associated with the disease. It's a very challenging condition to treat," says dental surgeon Nídia Cristina Castro dos Santos, the first author of the study and a professor and researcher at Einstein.

The researchers randomly divided the participants into four treatment groups. Every patient received subgingival instrumentation, commonly referred to as scaling. This standard periodontal treatment involves removing bacterial deposits and hardened plaque from tooth surfaces beneath the gums. Each group also received a different complementary treatment.

Patients in the control group received inactive substitutes for the antibiotics, omega-3, and aspirin, supplied in capsules that looked identical to those containing the active treatments.

A second group received metronidazole and amoxicillin three times daily for 14 days. This combination of antibiotics has some of the strongest scientific evidence supporting its use as an additional treatment for severe periodontitis.

Participants in the third group took three grams of omega-3 each day, together with a daily dose of low-dose aspirin, for six months. The fourth group received both interventions, taking antibiotics for two weeks while following the six-month omega-3 and aspirin regimen.

The researchers assessed the patients' progress at three, six, and 12 months.

At the end of the study, approximately 58% of patients in the antibiotic group had reached the researchers' clinical treatment target, defined as having no more than four remaining deep periodontal pockets.

The omega-3 and aspirin group achieved an almost identical success rate of 57.7%. By comparison, only 23.1% of patients who underwent scaling and received placebos reached the same target. Interestingly, administering both antibiotics and the omega-3 and aspirin regimen together did not produce any additional benefits.

Although antibiotics can improve treatment outcomes in patients with particularly severe gum disease, they are not routinely necessary for everyone with periodontitis.

"The use of antibiotics isn't considered the gold standard of treatment. Although metronidazole and amoxicillin yield good results in the most severe cases, their use should be evaluated on a case-by-case basis due to risks related to bacterial resistance and possible adverse effects," says Castro dos Santos.

Helping the Body Naturally Resolve Inflammation

The findings build on earlier research into the potential role of omega-3 fatty acids in protecting oral health. In a previous investigation, also supported by FAPESP and published in Scientific Reports, scientists found that omega-3 supplementation reduced periodontal inflammation and bone loss in rats. The protective effects were particularly notable when supplementation was combined with physical exercise.

Although results from animal studies do not necessarily translate directly to humans, the earlier findings provided clues that omega-3 might help regulate the inflammatory processes that contribute to gum disease.

Omega-3 fatty acids are a group of fats found in foods such as oily fish and are widely available as dietary supplements. Beyond their nutritional importance, they serve as building blocks for certain molecules that help regulate inflammation.

Castro explains that omega-3 works differently from conventional anti-inflammatory medications. Instead of simply interfering with pathways that promote inflammation, omega-3 helps the body produce molecules involved in bringing inflammation to a natural conclusion and supporting tissue repair.

This process, known as the resolution of inflammation, is an active biological mechanism that helps the body return to normal after an immune response. In chronic inflammatory diseases such as periodontitis, inflammation can persist and contribute to ongoing tissue damage.

The researchers included low-dose aspirin because it can promote the formation of certain inflammation-resolving molecules. They suspected that combining aspirin with omega-3 could strengthen the body's ability to control the persistent inflammation associated with advanced gum disease.

The researchers had originally expected antibiotics and the omega-3 regimen to work best when administered together. Instead, the findings revealed that targeting inflammation could produce clinical improvements comparable to those achieved through antibiotic treatment.

"We imagined that the combination of antibiotics and omega-3 would be most effective in controlling periodontitis in these patients. We also believed that the results for the group that used omega-3 with ASA would be slightly lower than those for the antibiotic group. The result was surprising because the two therapies performed very similarly, paving the way for it to become a treatment option for these patients," says Castro.

Equally intriguing was how long the improvements lasted. Six months after patients stopped taking omega-3 and aspirin, their clinical outcomes remained similar to those observed when the treatment ended.

According to Castro, this persistence raises the possibility that adjusting the body's inflammatory response could have lasting therapeutic effects. However, scientists are still working to understand the biological mechanisms responsible.

A Potential Alternative Amid Rising Antibiotic Resistance

For dental surgeon Magda Feres, the study's lead author and a full professor at the Harvard School of Dental Medicine and the Graduate Program in Dentistry at UNG, targeting the body's inflammatory response could provide a valuable treatment option for certain patients.

"The combination of omega-3 and low-dose aspirin achieved clinical benefits comparable to those of the metronidazole and amoxicillin protocol, opening up a real alternative for those who can't take antibiotics, especially patients with allergies or intolerance to these medications," she says.

The potential to reduce antibiotic use has implications that extend well beyond dentistry. Antibiotic resistance ranks among the greatest threats to global public health, making it increasingly important to identify effective treatment strategies that do not depend on these medications.

"Demonstrating that it's possible to treat severe periodontitis by modulating the body's own response is new and relevant information that helps preserve antibiotics for when they are truly indispensable," says Feres.

More Research Is Needed Before Clinical Practice Changes

Despite the encouraging findings, the researchers caution that the results are not sufficient to justify an immediate change in how dentists treat severe periodontitis. The participants did not have other significant systemic or oral diseases, meaning the results may not apply equally to patients with additional health conditions.

Larger studies involving more diverse populations will be needed to validate the findings and determine which patients are most likely to benefit from each treatment strategy.

It is also important to recognize that omega-3 and aspirin were used alongside professional periodontal treatment, rather than as a substitute for it. Aspirin carries potential risks, including an increased risk of bleeding, and may not be appropriate for everyone.

Meanwhile, Feres and her colleagues are investigating how the different treatments affect the communities of bacteria living inside periodontal pockets. Early microbiological findings point to a decline in bacterial species associated with periodontal disease and an increase in microorganisms linked to healthier gums.

These ongoing investigations could help explain why targeting inflammation produced such promising results and whether the approach can reliably benefit a broader range of patients.

"It's an important step forward, but not the end of the story. Therefore, the message is one of cautious optimism: we have a promising, scientifically plausible alternative to antibiotics in select cases. Routine replacement will require more evidence," she concludes.

#4252. Nongshim RedForce sign Deft after military service, reuniting DRX’s 2022 world title trio

Nongshim RedForce have brought 2022 world champion Deft back to the LCK and paired him again with Kingen and Pyosik. The move follows an eighth-place 2026 for the club and comes days after BLG ended Korea's four-year hold on the World Championship.

Kim ‘Deft’ Hyuk-kyu’s signing was confirmed on 19 November. The club used its official social media channels to make the announcement. Deft began his military service after the 2024 season ended.

The deal reunites him with two members of the DRX side that won the 2022 World Championship. Jungler Hong ‘Pyosik’ Chang-hyeon joined later the same day, alongside support Moon ‘Andil’ Gwan-bin. Top laner Hwang ‘Kingen’ Seong-hoon had re-signed a day earlier.

Deft’s signing was announced at 7pm. The Pyosik and Andil additions that followed completed Nongshim’s five-man starting line-up, Inven Global reported. Mid laner Seon ‘Calix’ Hyeon-bin provides continuity. He has been with the organisation since 2021 and extended his deal on 18 November.

Deft brings a long winning record. He made his debut with MVP Blue in 2013. His titles include the LCK, the LPL, the Mid-Season Invitational and the 2022 World Championship.

Kingen first joined Nongshim for the 2025 season. Pyosik arrives after a difficult 2026 at DN SOOPers. That team lost a run of matches, and rookie Sharvel took his starting place.

The move had been signalled. About a month before the announcement, Sheep Esports reported from Korean sources that Nongshim planned to sign Deft. The same report said rookie AD carry Diable would need a new team.

The signings mark a sharp change of direction after a poor year. Once the league campaign was over, the team lasted just a single match in the play-ins.

The deal lands days after a setback for the whole league. Bilibili Gaming’s victory over Gen.G came at the Barclays Center in New York. It gave the organisation its first Summoner’s Cup.

BLG won all four of its series against LCK teams at the tournament. Every LCK seed fell to the Chinese side on its way to the trophy. The title is also the LPL’s first since EDward Gaming won in 2021.

'Deft' has signed a contract as the new ADC of NS RedForce LCK Team.

Please look forward to and support Deft, who has written new history with an unbreakable spirit through countless trials, as he takes on new challenges and delivers great… pic.twitter.com/bHa1uJWwKV

#4251. Battlefield 6’s first big map in months is coming to Labs soon, but I'm more excited about BF4's Golmud Railway making its way to BF6

As promised, Battlefield Labs is coming back to bring us a preview of some of Battlefield 6’s upcoming Season 2 content.

Battlefield 6’s Season 2 was recently pushed back by a month to give Battlefield Studios time to polish up its content. Now, the developer has revealed how it plans to use some of that time, and the first port of call is Battlefield Labs.

As discussed in the initial delay message, BF Studios wants the community’s involvement earlier and more consistently in the development of future content. This includes Season 2, of course, and a big component of what it’s bringing to the game is headed to Labs.

The first Battlefield Labs session kicking off soon will focus on Contaminated, one of the new maps coming to Battlefield 6 with Season 2. BF Studios says the map falls between Eastwood and Mirak Valley, in terms of size.

The blog post even likened it to Battlefield 1’s St. Quentin Scar, and Battlefield 5’s Arras. Although we’ve yet to actually play it, the size and description do sound really well, especially in a game as starved of big maps as Battlefield 6 currently is.

Another thing BF Studios wants to test is the way ground vehicle gameplay and aerial presence interact with infantry combat, which is pretty standard for most Battlefield maps. Interestingly, there appears to be some sort of mechanic unique to Contaminated that the developer also wants to evaluate.

More Labs sessions are planned, including one that will show off new gameplay tools and vehicles. The AH-6 Little Bird helicopter was specifically namedropped, which makes sense given that it’s going to be part of Season 2’s content.

Battlefield Labs sessions will also extend beyond the biggest-ticket items of maps and vehicles. BF Studios said we should expect tests of upcoming features, like the Aircraft Radar, as part of a list of other air combat updates.

Ground vehicles, and they way the various rockets interact with them, will also be evaluated in a different session, with specific adjustments planned for RPGs and TOWs. And, of course, the work to improve and perfect hit reg remains ongoing, and future tweaks will go through Labs first.

There’s even more exciting news for fans of big maps, as the blog post also confirmed that Battlefield 4’s Golmud Railway is currently in the works, planned to go live in a future season. Golmud Railway will show up early in Labs, and you can expect it to evolve over multiple sessions.

For context, when it does arrive in Battlefield 6, Golmud Railway will be the largest map in the game, which is saying something. Though the map is beloved by vehicle players, it has its issues elsewhere, and BF Studios says it will be looking at all that when it creates the BF6, emphasising that it won’t be a simple port of the BF4 original.

Finally, the post throws a bone to Redsec battle royale players still waiting for a Solo mode. BF Studios continues to test the idea internally, but it’s taking a while. Needless to say, there are so many aspects that need to be considered. Game pace, balance, player survivability, match flow just to name a few.

Redsec BR was built with squads in mind, so that task is extra challenging. Though the developer didn’t say when we can expect Solos to arrive in Labs, players will get a chance to experience it before it enters the live game.

#4250. A fat-burning molecule has an unexpected benefit for your muscles

Researchers have identified a naturally occurring molecule that plays a crucial role in building muscle strength and improving physical performance. Released during exercise, the molecule could also provide the basis for future treatments to protect against muscle damage associated with type 2 diabetes.

The molecule, known as L-β-aminoisobutyric acid (L-BAIBA), is essential for muscles to adapt to physical activity. It helps muscles become stronger, improves their resistance to fatigue, and protects against damage and weakness.

The study, published in Nature Communications and funded by Diabetes UK and the Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council (BBSRC), reveals that L-BAIBA is a central regulator of the biological changes that allow muscles to improve their strength, structure, and endurance in response to exercise training.

How Exercise Triggers a Natural Muscle Booster

Although the health benefits of exercise are well established, scientists still do not fully understand the biological processes that allow the body to adapt to physical demands. A research team led by Professor Lee Roberts at the University of Leeds investigated whether these processes could reveal new ways to treat chronic conditions such as type 2 diabetes.

L-BAIBA has attracted scientific interest for more than a decade. In research published in 2014, Roberts demonstrated that the molecule has beneficial effects on metabolism, helping to enhance the body's ability to burn fat in response to exercise. L-BAIBA is now commercially available as a dietary supplement.

The latest findings reveal another important function of the molecule. L-BAIBA acts as a chemical messenger that connects physical activity with beneficial changes in muscle structure and metabolism, helping muscles adapt to the demands placed on them.

Lee Roberts, Professor of Molecular Physiology and Metabolism at the University of Leeds, said: "Our research identifies L-BAIBA as an exercise-induced signal that helps muscles adapt, improve their metabolic capacity and ability to contract, and ultimately enhances physical performance.

"This gives us exciting new insight into how exercise benefits the body and highlights a promising target for future therapies aimed at preserving muscle function in chronic conditions such as diabetes."

Protecting Muscles Against Damage From Type 2 Diabetes

The researchers also discovered that L-BAIBA protects muscles against damage associated with type 2 diabetes. The condition can negatively affect muscle health, leading to a decline in muscle mass and strength, as well as disruptions in the way muscles process and use energy. These complications can significantly reduce a person's quality of life.

Because regular physical activity is an important part of managing type 2 diabetes, finding ways to improve muscle function and reduce fatigue could make a substantial difference for people who struggle to exercise.

Type 2 diabetes is a serious chronic condition that increases the risk of potentially life-threatening complications, including heart attacks and strokes. Its development is influenced by a complex combination of factors, including age, ethnicity, genetics, and living with overweight or obesity.

Although type 2 diabetes has traditionally been more common among older adults, diagnoses in people younger than 40 have been rising in recent years. Cases in this younger age group are now increasing more rapidly than among adults over 40.

A Promising Target for Future Diabetes Treatments

Anna Morris, Assistant Director of Research Strategy and Partnership at Diabetes UK, said: "Exercise plays an important role in managing type 2 diabetes, but for many people muscle weakness and fatigue can make staying active a real challenge. This research helps us better understand how muscles adapt to exercise and identifies a potential new target for improving muscle health. While these findings are still at an early stage, they could help shape future approaches that support people with type 2 diabetes to remain active and live healthier, longer lives."

Although the discovery opens promising avenues for future treatments, further research is needed to determine whether L-BAIBA supplementation can produce meaningful therapeutic benefits in people with type 2 diabetes.

The research was led by the University of Leeds in collaboration with:

The study was funded by Diabetes UK and BBSRC.

#4248. Shopify Rebellion Black beat Xora 2-0 in opening VCT Americas Kickoff qualifier match

Shopify Rebellion Black opened the North America Qualifier Playoffs with a 2-0 win over Xora Esports. The non-partner organisation is now one win from the playoffs that decide a guaranteed São Paulo Kickoff place.

The best-of-three Group Stage meeting with Xora began at 00:10 UTC on Saturday 21 November, opening Shopify Rebellion Black’s VCT Americas Kickoff: North America 2027 campaign.

The result counts for more because Shopify Rebellion is now outside Riot’s partnership system. The organisation was one of the Americas sides that said it had not been chosen for the 2027-2028 partnership programme, Sheep Esports reported. Cloud9, ENVY, M80, FlyQuest and LYON were also on that list. Riot now has eight partner teams in each of its four regions.

The Swiss Stage runs from 20 to 22 November 2026. Every match is best of three. Two wins send a team through to the playoffs, and two losses knock it out. The eight teams left after the Swiss phase move into a double-elimination bracket played over six competition days, with the playoffs set for 1 to 6 December. The event is listed as an online, A-Tier Riot Games qualifier for 16 teams.

Shopify Rebellion Black’s next opponents are Oafs, who also won their opening match 2-0, against QoR. Both teams are therefore one win from the playoffs. Oafs already have a record against Xora. They knocked them out of the Qualifier 1 bracket on 8 November with a 2-1 win. Xora had still reached the Qualifier Playoffs by finishing joint third in the 512-team North America Qualifier 1.

Across 83 rated matches, Shopify Rebellion Black hold a 59-24 record. Before this event their most recent series was a 2-3 defeat to 2GAME Esports at the VCL Americas Last Chance Qualifier 2026. Earlier in that event they had beaten 2GAME Esports 2-1 and Contra 2-0.

The organisation’s second line-up had a harder start. Shopify Rebellion Gold lost 0-2 to Maryville University. Several of the other organisations left out of the partnership programme won their first matches. Cloud9 beat counterfeit 2-0, Team Envy beat Yellow Dragon Gaming 2-0 and FlyQuest edged Masterclass 2-1. Elsewhere, Winthrop University beat SaD Esports 2-0 and YFP Gaming beat Wildcard 2-1.

The prize for coming through the bracket is a place in São Paulo. Riot will stage the 2027 VCT Americas Kickoff in Brazil. Its eight Partner Teams get direct entry. Non-partner teams can win four places: one guaranteed slot each for North America, Brazil and Latin America, plus one for the Americas Last Chance Qualifier. For a non-partner side, a later run to Masters would be worth a fixed US$200,000 and a place at Champions US$400,000, Dot Esports reported. The regional Kickoff events are due to start on 14 January 2027 and run until 7 February 2027.

#4247. Arc Raiders finally reveals early 2026 roadmap, but we’re not getting a new map for a while

The first couple of months of 2026 in the world of Arc Raiders look pretty promising, but the big guns are being held back for now.

After weeks of waiting, Arc Raiders developer Embark has officially unveiled the first few months of the game’s 2026 roadmap. The plan is split into four months, covering January to April, collectively dubbed Escalation.

We’re expecting a content update each month, with the majority of the biggest additions happening on the game’s existing maps. There is, however, at least one new map in the works, but it won’t be here until sometime in April.

While we wait for that, Arc Raiders is going to go through several events and other in-game changes, some more meaningful (and exciting) than others. January looks to be the lightest so far, which makes sense given that it’s just a week or so from ending.

January’s chapter is titled Headwinds, kicking off on January 27. This segment will see the addition of a new matchmaking option for players above level 40 - at or near the game’s endgame. We’re also expecting a new Map Condition, and a new Player Project for everyone to contribute to.

Things start getting interesting in February, when Shrouded Sky will begin. This chapter brings three exciting additions to Arc Raiders. There will be a new Map Condition, new Arc Threat, and the start of another Player Project.

Interestingly, we’re going to see some sort of map update during the month, but Embark didn’t share anymore details. The next Raider Deck will also deploy in February, alongside a new Expedition Window.

The Flashpoint chapter begins in March, when we’re expecting another new Map Condition, one more new Arc Threat, as well as another Player Project. March’s most interesting addition is an update to everyone’s trusty rooster friend, Scrappy.

Finally, April is when the big guns come out, because that’s when the first new map of 2026 will arrive in Arc Raiders. With it, comes a new large Arc, which is to be expected. A new Map Condition will debut then, too, likely starting off on the new map.

That’s pretty much it, but seeing as we’re just one day away from the start of the January stage, things are about to get exciting again in Arc Raiders.

#4246. Harvard’s tiny UV light chip could help shrink quantum computers

Ultraviolet (UV) light is already essential to a wide range of modern technologies. Beyond its natural presence in sunlight, it is used to disinfect surfaces, make biological materials fluoresce, and manufacture computer chips through a process called photolithography. In the future, microscopic sources of UV light built directly into photonic chips could enable smaller quantum computers, ultra-precise atomic clocks, and other advanced technologies.

However, shrinking UV light sources to fit on a chip has presented a significant engineering challenge. Ultraviolet light rapidly loses power as it travels through optical waveguides, the tiny channels that carry light across a chip. This limitation has made it extremely difficult to develop compact UV sources with enough power for practical applications.

Now, a Harvard-led research team has demonstrated a microscopic photonic device that produces approximately 120 times more UV power than previous comparable devices. The researchers, working in the laboratory of Marko Lončar, the Tiantsai Lin Professor of Electrical Engineering, achieved the breakthrough using a widely studied material called thin-film lithium niobate.

Published in Nature Communications, the findings establish lithium niobate as a promising platform for generating powerful ultraviolet light in compact devices while minimizing optical losses.

Rather than trying to deliver ultraviolet light directly through microscopic channels, the researchers designed a device that generates UV light from red light within the chip itself.

The approach relies on a process known as frequency upconversion. Inside the lithium niobate crystal, two photons of red light combine to produce a single ultraviolet photon with higher energy. Lithium niobate is particularly well suited to this process because of its exceptional ability to convert light from one frequency to another.

"Our group is perhaps best known for utilizing lithium niobate for photonic devices that operate at longer, infrared wavelengths -- closer to the realm of telecommunications signals," Lončar said.

However, the team found that this transparent crystalline material, which has become increasingly important in integrated photonics, can also support light sources and guide light at much shorter wavelengths, including those in the ultraviolet range.

"When people think about [thin-film lithium niobate], they don't think of it as a UV material, but we show that it is," said co-first author Kees Franken, former research fellow in the Lončar lab. "We also show that there are some other nonlinear effects happening that we don't fully understand yet."

A New Technique Overcomes a Major Engineering Barrier

The device uses optical waveguides, microscopic channels etched into the lithium niobate film that direct light through the chip in much the same way electrical wires carry current.

For red light to be efficiently converted into ultraviolet light, the orientation of regions within the crystal must be repeatedly reversed at precisely controlled intervals along the waveguide. This manufacturing process, called poling, is a specialized technique used in nonlinear optics.

One of the biggest challenges has been creating these patterns with accuracy at scales smaller than a micrometer across devices that extend for centimeters.

Previous manufacturing methods required researchers to make an undesirable compromise. Poling the entire film before forming the waveguides made it difficult to correct manufacturing imperfections. Alternatively, creating the waveguides first reduced conversion efficiency because the electrodes were positioned too far away, allowing only part of the film to be successfully poled.

To eliminate this tradeoff, the Harvard team developed a technique they call "sidewall poling."

Precision Engineering Dramatically Improves Light Conversion

Instead of positioning the electrodes exclusively above the lithium niobate film, the researchers placed precisely patterned metal structures resembling tiny fingers directly alongside the etched waveguide. During fabrication, they applied a small voltage to permanently reverse the orientation of the crystal domains in a carefully controlled pattern.

"The key idea was: could we just put the electrodes directly on the waveguide?" said co-first author and former graduate student Soumya Ghosh. "It's a high-precision fabrication process to position the electrodes but requiring about 50-nanometer accuracy."

This arrangement enabled the researchers to reverse the crystal domains throughout the entire cross section of the waveguide, allowing light traveling through the material to undergo much more efficient frequency conversion.

The team could also fine-tune the spacing of the reversed crystal regions along the device. By incorporating existing "adapted poling" techniques previously developed in Lončar's laboratory and elsewhere, the researchers compensated for variations in the thickness of the lithium niobate film and the shape of the waveguide.

The resulting device generated 4.2 milliwatts of ultraviolet power directly on the chip at a wavelength of 390 nanometers. That represents approximately 120 times the output power achieved by the best previous thin-film lithium niobate devices operating in this wavelength range.

Earlier experiments using the material generated only tens of microwatts of UV power. Although those results demonstrated that the approach was scientifically feasible, the output was too low to support practical applications.

The substantial increase in power could be particularly valuable for trapped-ion quantum computers. These machines use electrically charged atoms to store and process quantum information. Many of the specific atomic energy transitions required to operate them involve light in the near-ultraviolet portion of the spectrum.

"If you want a scalable quantum computer that isn't the size of a truck, you need to scale everything down to the chip level, and this includes the light sources," Franken said.

The technology could also benefit ultra-precise atomic clocks and environmental monitoring systems. According to the researchers, the same range of ultraviolet wavelengths is well suited to compact sensors designed to closely monitor greenhouse gases and other atmospheric pollutants.

Franken and Ghosh attribute the breakthrough partly to the collaborative structure of Lončar's laboratory, where researchers carry out every stage of device development in one place, including theoretical research, engineering design, cleanroom fabrication, and optical testing.

"The hands-on intuition that we gained for how to make a device, while also keeping the zoomed-out view of what this device is for, and how we were going to characterize it -- that's a big part of what enabled this project for us," Ghosh said.

"Milliwatt-level UV generation using sidewall poled lithium niobate" was further co-authored by C.C. Rodrigues, J. Yang, C.J. Xin, S. Lu, D. Witt, G. Joe, G.S. Wiederhecker, and K.-J. Boller.

U.S. federal funding for the project came from the following sources: Department of the Air Force grant No. FA9453-23-C-A039; Office of Naval Research grant No. N00014-22-C-1041/VAS-21-0001; NASA grant No. 80NSSC22K0262 and 80NSSC23PB442; and National Science Foundation grants ERC EEC-1941583 and OMA-2137723.

Materials provided by Harvard John A. Paulson School of Engineering and Applied Sciences. Original written by Anne J. Manning. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#4245. The First GTA 6 DLC is Now Live for All Players

If you missed out on the Grand Theft Auto 6 pre-order bonuses, Rockstar is now offering the Vintage Vice City Pack as a standalone purchase. It's available on PS5 and Xbox Series X|S. The DLC, which includes a classic car, a garage and some particularly nostalgic outfits, costs $4.99 in the US on both consoles.

Download GTA 6's official Leonida map and printable cover art free from Rockstar. Here's where to find them and how the physical poster differs.

According to Rockstar's original pre-order announcement, the pack was included with pre-orders of both editions of GTA 6, as well as digital purchases made before November 20. That meant you could still get the bonus if you bought the game on launch day. If you picked up your copy over the weekend instead, you'll have to pay for the extra content.

According to the official Xbox Store listing, the Vintage Vice City Pack went on sale as a separate add-on on November 20. It isn't a story expansion, but it does offer a little more than just cosmetic items for Jason and Lucia.

The most useful part of the pack is arguably the garage. It's located at Shore Court, near Ocean Beach, and comes with a weapon locker and storage space for goods you've stolen and intend to sell to a fence. You also get a 1955 Vapid Stanier, a classic sedan to keep in the garage. The extra garage alone might make the pack worthwhile if you like collecting cars in GTA.

The extra garage alone might make the pack worthwhile if you like collecting cars in GTA.

As for the cosmetic items, Jason gets a pastel linen suit and a retro haircut, while Lucia gets a short red sequin dress and curly hair. There's also a tropical weapon skin that you can apply to most firearms. The design is based on Tommy Vercetti's unmistakable Hawaiian shirt from GTA Vice City, which is a nice little detail for those of us who grew up playing that game.

The funny thing is that you can already unlock Tommy's original shirt in GTA 6 without buying anything extra. The catch is that it involves a rather elaborate Easter egg, so you might want to set aside some time for that one.

Before spending another five dollars on GTA 6, it's worth checking whether you already own the pack. The outfits, vehicle and garage don't all become available the moment you start the game. You'll have to reach certain points in Jason and Lucia's story before you can claim them.

Rockstar published a support article on November 24 explaining how to access the pre-order rewards. Bring up the pause menu, head to the Store section and find the Vintage Vice City Pack. Selecting an individual reward will tell you what you need to do to unlock it, so you don't have to guess which chapter you should be in. Once you've met the requirements, you'll have to return to the game itself to claim the reward. The Store menu tells you how to get it rather than handing you the items directly.

You don't need the Ultimate Edition to use the Vintage Vice City Pack, either. If you bought the Standard Edition on launch day, for instance, you should check your existing rewards rather than assume the pack is exclusive to the more expensive edition. It's sold separately from the Ultimate Edition Upgrade, and the latter has its own selection of unlockable vehicles, clothing and weapons.

GTA 4 gave us two excellent single-player expansions in The Lost and Damned and The Ballad of Gay Tony, and we never got anything comparable for GTA 5 despite its ridiculously long lifespan.

Hopefully, Rockstar has something more substantial planned for GTA 6's single-player DLC. As much as I appreciate the nods to Vice City, I'd love to see the series return to the kind of expansions we got with GTA 4.

Like many games, Grand Theft Auto 6 is full of easter eggs for you to discover. These are some of the best Leonida has to offer.

#4244. The Video Games And More You Should Play This Weekend – November 13, 2026

Today is Friday the 13th, but let's not dwell on that. Here are some weekend video games to play. Well, actually, here are some of our biggest stories of the week, and then you can check out some weekend game recommendations.

Also, go ahead and make some space on your Xbox or PlayStation hard drive to make room for GTAVI. It's going to be about 200 GB and you can pre-load it now. Delete those games you're not going to return to. Delete all those video clips you'll never watch from every time you get a Trophy on your PlayStation. And you know what? Go ahead and delete Fortnite, too. It's time.

Calling all sickos of The Rootrees Are Dead, Return of the Obra Dinn, The Incident At Galley House, and everything in between: there’s another good deduction game to obsess over. Funeral for the Sun stars a historian who visits an abandoned Latin American town to piece together its turbulent history, chiefly the truth behind the mysterious disappearance of its hundreds of residents (who were, officially speaking, lost in a fire). Supernatural forces allow players to peer into the town’s past to learn about key people potentially responsible for the calamity, who they must identify by name, establish relationships between, and even match younger and older versions of themselves. You even keep track of information using a multi-function notebook à la The Roottrees Are Dead. Boasting an enticing story, a beautiful painterly art direction, and a tight runtime at roughly 8-hours (or less if you’re really on a roll), Funeral for the Sun is a mystery worth unraveling if you need a new deduction game to cozy up with.

NetEase has continued to impress with the pace and quality of its regular updates to Marvel Rivals, which continues today with the release of an 11th season for the superhero battler. Right here at launch, the notable addition is he arrival of X-Men hero Nightcrawler, who BAMFs his way into battle as a strategist, equally capable of healing allies and taking out foes with his sword and brimstone bombs. As is almost always the case right at a new hero’s launch, it can be hard to snag him on the roster on opening day to see how he plays, but once you do, I expect you’ll find him a versatile healer who can pretty dramatically shake up the battlefield, especially with his Ultimate, which basically consolidates allies and enemies together in one central clump for a frenzied exchange of blows. Alongside the new batch of seasonal cosmetics and events to dive into, it’s once again a good time to don your hero outfit and take on some matches.

Pikmin 4 released on Switch 2 this week (or upgraded to Switch 2 depending on how you look at it), and that's a good thing. Pikmin 4 is the best game in the series and the Switch 2 version is the best version. That's great for those who never finished the game (your save does transfer) or skipped Pikmin 4 when it released in 2023, but if you're looking for an excuse to return to the game and play new content, the Dandori Academy addition is underwhelming. You can read my full thoughts here.

Metaphor: ReFantazio, originally released in 2024, is a great RPG from the creators of Persona. And the Persona lineage is obvious throughout the full game. You have to pick and choose where and with whom you should be spending your time, all while a big world-saving RPG with a memorable party of characters plays out in the foreground.

It released this week for Switch 2 and it’s a game that I think would play well on a handheld device. It’s also just a good RPG to play if you missed it previously.

Fun fact: Metaphor: ReFantazio was the game we had lined up to be the next cover when we were temporarily shut down in in 2024. We went to the studio and had a cover drawn up and everything. You can read the full details of the cover story that never was right here.

You can also read Game Informer's review of Metaphor: ReFantazio by following the link.

As we enjoy the final week in a pre-GTA VI world, what better way to gird your loins for next week’s release, so to speak, than by revisiting the last adventures set in Rockstar’s take on Miami? 2002’s Grand Theft Auto: Vice City is a certified classic that, if you’ve never played it, offers nice foundational insight into what Vice City was like in the ’80s (spoiler: it was a lot like Scarface and Miami Vice). Best of all, Vice City is easily available on current platforms with modernized improvements to boot.

If you want to go even further back, chronologically speaking, Grand Theft Auto: Vice City Stories is a prequel set two years before the events of Vice City. Maybe, in some extremely minute way, Vice City Stories lays narrative groundwork for GTA VI. It’s unlikely, but you never know. Originally released for PSP in 2006, Vice City Stories is trickier to play if you don’t own Sony's retired handheld or a PlayStation 2, which it was ported to in 2007. But if you can find the means, there’s no better time to check out this often overlooked chapter of Vice City’s history.

I usually hold off on early access games, to preserve my experience for the finished product, but I just couldn’t resist Slay the Spire 2. The co-op gameplay is an awesome, major change, but even just adding a couple of new characters and cards would have satisfied my cravings. To that end, this week’s free update adds a brand new character, the Fool, who I’m eager to test out.

FYI, this new character is only available on the game’s beta, so you’ll have to go into the game settings on steam, click Properties, then Game Versions & Betas, and then opt into the “public-beta” version of the game to check the new content out. The patch notes for this update specifically say, “We expect to make a great number of content and balance changes before the Fool is ready for the main branch,” so expect frequent tweaks and a bit of a wait before the Fool joins the main Early Access branch. The new beta update also adds two more game modes: Dread and Blitz, which drastically alter your runs. If you want to wait a little while, the team at Mega Crit will refine these options into a more final form. But if you’re like me, more Slay the Spire 2 is more Slay the Spire 2, and I’m hopping in as soon as I can.

Monster Train 2 was one of my favorite games of last year, so I’m always glad to have a reason to jump back in. This week’s DLC, The Punished, is a perfect opportunity to do so, adding a new clan to the base game’s already packed roster. Since any clan can be combined with a second one to start a run, adding just one more option at the game’s start has an exponential effect, expanding the ways you can approach each attempt. As the DLC’s name implies, the new Punished clan gains buffs when taking damage, and you get new suite of cards that damages the whole playing field at once, harming foes and bolstering your allies. Even if you’re not checking out the DLC, the base game is absolutely worth picking up – just read my glowing review.

If you’ve been hankering for a new direction to go with your tabletop RPG group, may I recommend the incredibly versatile Cypher System from Monte Cook Games? The new Character Rulebook includes everything you need to get started, and set your adventures in virtually any fictional backdrop you can imagine, from hard sci-fi to gritty horror to high fantasy. Cypher’s polished approach to narrative-first and player-focused game sessions is much easier to pick up than many new rules systems, but it has enormous flexibility to deliver smart, creative, and exciting adventures that can help to change things up if your playing group has been in a rut.

#4243. Xenogears Is Finally Getting Remastered, But Not in the Way You Think

Murillo Zerbinatto is a JRPG enthusiast, writer, and editor. He has played over 300 RPGs during his gaming career, with 90% of them being JRPGs.

There are two perspectives on remasters and remakes. On one hand, we have those who complain whenever a developer announces a new one, wishing they would dedicate development efforts to bringing new IPs to life. On the other hand, we have those who rejoice and feel the nostalgia tingling whenever a game that shaped their tastes returns to the modern era. I fall into the latter camp, which is why I am extremely excited for the upcoming fanmade remaster of Xenogears.

The Elder Scrolls Travels: Shadowkey, the long-forgotten Nokia N-Gage RPG, is returning!

To be fair, three Xenogears remasters are currently being developed by fans, each with its own codename: Weltall, Exodus, and Atlas. Today I'll discuss the Atlas remaster because it seems to be the one the fanbase is most excited about, and it already has an imminent release date of 15 December 2026. However, keep in mind that since this is not an official remaster from Square Enix, you can only legally play it if you own an original copy of Xenogears at home.

The project could hardly be called a Xenogears remaster if it didn't include notable upgrades over the original. According to the creator, Reddit user Ok-Bed3203, the entire game has been rebuilt in the Godot engine and will run directly inside it, provided you supply your own copy of the game. Fans can experience Xenogears Atlas in two distinct visual styles, dubbed Canon and HD.

In Canon mode, the visuals remain faithful to the 1998 release, while incorporating technical fixes such as eliminating flickering triangles or textures, stabilizing sprites and images, and smoothing out screen fades. Meanwhile, High Definition mode introduces enhanced textures and sprites, 16:9 widescreen support (with menus, text, and FMVs preserved in their original 4:3 framing so nothing gets stretched), updated lighting and visual effects, and 3D Gears.

Both modes will support 60 FPS, 120 FPS, or your monitor's native refresh rate. They also include 2K CG cutscenes upscaled by Laichzeit (likely exclusive to HD mode, though not explicitly specified), subtitles in every language, fan translations, and quality-of-life options like text speed adjustments, quick loads, full-screen or windowed modes, and automatic pausing when running in the background.

Independent developer LoreanXavier, also known as Lorean The Gamer, has been working on an unofficial native PC port of P.T. for quite some time.

After the initial release, the developers plan to add a Mods menu that lets you load custom text patches and swap images or audio files by name, along with remastered music from Xenogears' iconic soundtrack and further touch-ups to the 2K movies. The community has also suggested several additions currently under consideration, including random encounter rate toggles, a reduced-flash mode, auto-advancing dialogue, optional voice-over via the Spoken Mirror fan dub (slated to arrive alongside the Disc 2 remake), and a dedicated Android port.

As you probably noticed, the developer mentioned a Disc 2 remake. That sounds like a tall order, because as anyone who played the game remembers, Xenogears features a pristine Disc 1, whereas the second disc was famously rushed after Square cut the budget before the project could be finished, which severely undermined the experience. Atlas aims to give Disc 2 the breathing room it never received. While it is not yet completely clear what that will entail or when it will arrive, it is easily the most intriguing prospect of this entire fanmade remaster.

While the project looks incredible and has me thoroughly hyped, one looming question always hangs in the air these days: was this project made using AI? The developer preemptively addressed that very concern:

“About AI, since it always comes up: yes, I used AI as a tool along the way, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. But this is not a vibe-coded project. I checked every cutscene, every movement and every 16:9 margin by hand, then fixed it and compared it with the original. A huge part of the work was the boring part: tracking down the smallest glitches left over from the PS1 renderer, one by one, until they were gone. Monk work, honestly. I hope you'll feel it when you play.”

About AI, since it always comes up: yes, I used AI as a tool along the way, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise.

So there you have it. If you want to experience or revisit Xenogears with revamped visuals, quality-of-life additions, tweaks, and technical fixes, Xenogears Atlas might just be the way to go. This Xenogears remaster launches on 15 December 2026, via Godot for PC, though you will still need your original copy to get it running. Who knows, maybe this will finally wake Square Enix up to greenlight a full-fledged official remaster, or at least sell the IP back to Tetsuya Takahashi.

These are 10 PS1 JRPGs that are still trapped on the original hardware and would certainly benefit from a modern port.
