#4179. 7 Details That Make GTA 6 A Flawed Game

Ronald is a video game journalist with more than 10 years of experience in the industry, working on several of the most important Spanish websites.

GTA 6 has become the highest-rated video game of all time according to Metacritic, sparking debate about whether it truly represents the closest thing to perfection in our history.

As someone who has enjoyed the series since the century's beginning, and who considers himself a huge fan of the Red Dead Redemption franchise, I have mixed feelings about this assertion, as the game's shortcomings are not hidden at any point.

Do these weaknesses diminish its revolutionary and utterly awe-inspiring nature? Not in the slightest, as it remains an extraordinary adventure that we will admire for decades, even with its imperfections.

Therefore, in order to discuss the game honestly and respectfully while also questioning the merits of its unparalleled achievements, here are seven details that make GTA 6 a flawed game.

Considering its draw distance, countless interactive elements, and dynamic entities that come alive in Leonida every second you walk, it's completely understandable that GTA 6 doesn't have a consistent frame rate.

Although this might say more about the platforms it was released on than the product itself, it certainly impacts the overall experience, especially in the most spectacular sequences where so many factors converge that the game seems on the verge of crashing.

As someone who grew up with such limited hardware that I had to play Hollow Knight at 15 FPS, I'd be lying if I said it was a negative aspect that bothered me too much, yet its easy and regularly noticeable nature is equally undeniable.

When the next-gen and PC versions arrive, I'm sure I'll have to update the article and remove this entry, but for now, it's the first drawback you notice, and it's impossible to ignore.

Striking the right pace for an open-world game's main story is among the most difficult tasks in the entire genre, as the chances of the player getting stuck, overwhelmed, or impatient are extremely high.

For better or worse, GTA 6 exposes itself to these pitfalls by presenting a campaign whose problem isn't necessarily its length, but rather the way many sections feel artificially stretched to reach such numbers.

The pacing is inconsistent, with entire hours of gameplay where the plot barely advances, only to have the entire storyline suddenly shift in specific moments, feeling like a vehicle accelerating and braking so hard it makes your back ache.

While Red Dead Redemption 2's story is roughly the same duration, Arthur Morgan's tale flows smoothly (let's forget about Guarma), and Jason and Lucia's, perhaps intentionally, suffer numerous ups and downs that disconnect you at times.

Grand Theft Auto 6 puts a large emphasis on keeping your relationship sound, so you need to know what ways are the best to raise the romance between Jason and Lucia.

Given GTA 6's size and complexity, the existence of bugs was entirely predictable, and it's rather surprising that, given the hardware, it doesn't include even more technical issues that hinder the player experience.

However, their presence occasionally transcends the anecdotal, with absurdly inconsistent autosaves that cause you to lose hours of progress, permanent weather conditions that don't change, NPCs that appear and disappear, and crashes that shut down the game without warning.

These are just what I've experienced firsthand, but reading anecdotes and watching footage shared online, it's clear that the plethora of errors is much greater, ranging from merely annoying to downright game-breaking.

It's light-years away from being like Cyberpunk 2077's launch, so the comparison is grossly unfair, but the fact that it's been a launch with irregularities is obvious and immediately apparent as soon as you start the game.

I admire the calm with which Rockstar chose to introduce us to the most anticipated video game in history, offering a prologue that, beyond mere formalities, actually extends to the end of Chapter 1.

The entire campaign, both narratively and in terms of gameplay, doesn't truly unfold until after 10 hours, during which you spend more time performing mundane tasks than interacting with GTA 6's rich systems.

Until then, the activities and objectives are quite limited, with few shootouts, no interactions with the police, minimal need for customization, and moderate interactions that only experience occasional bursts of intensity.

While I find this approach daring by AAA standards and think it's commendable, I believe that Colter in Red Dead Redemption 2 also has a slow start, yet with a far superior pace and impact, showing there's room for improvement.

As a result, since GTA 6 inherits its entire exoskeleton from Rockstar's latest release, I have no choice but to compare them directly, and it becomes clear which of the two does a better job of immersing the player in their first hours of gameplay.

This is a brief guide that entails the location of the Fast and Furious green Eclipse in GTA 6.

Since the studio hasn't lost its knack, understandable but erratic, for including dialogue in every commute, GTA 6 suffers from the same weakness that has plagued all the company's games for years.

I've lost count of how many times conversations between characters are interrupted because, since they're tied to the distance between two points, it's common to arrive quickly at your destination only to have the exchange end prematurely.

I know they introduced the option to read the conversation history from the pause menu, but for Rockstar to offer this as their solution to such a long-standing and annoying problem seems truly poor.

It might sound nitpicky, though it breaks the immersion and makes you miss parts of the plot and the relationships between characters, so it's not appropriate to underestimate the issue's magnitude.

Speaking of perpetuating past transgressions, it's surprising how the morality system is an idea replicated ad nauseam in the video game industry, yet virtually no one can implement it successfully.

In this case, you again have a spectrum that oscillates between being a saint or a devil based on specific actions that feel terribly gamified rather than immersive, as they're more of a checklist of behaviors and actions than a genuine human scale.

That petting a cat has a positive impact, just as robbing a drug caravan by only shooting dozens of thugs in the knees is an interesting way to approach the ethical behavior of our protagonists, who will still canonically steal and murder no matter how hard you try to be good.

It's an arbitrary and artificial metric, and while it's partially redeemed by being a measure of criminal professionalism rather than civic morality, it's difficult to reconcile such a realistic and captivating world with a system of emojis that determine your worth as a criminal.

Even just having the system work behind the scenes in accordance with our natural inclinations, like Dishonored, without forcing any kind of action but allowing us to discover the consequences of our moves organically, would be much better, so it feels like a missed opportunity.

Some players may think they should register a hot new sports car as their starter car. There's actually a better choice. Here's the best starter car to register in GTA VI.

Video games find in technology the key to their existence, as it's the mechanism that allows interaction and, therefore, gives meaning to these magical digital worlds in which we can completely blend ourselves.

Consequently, the fact that GTA 6 is the most impressive technical feat we've seen in the industry is enough to consider it revolutionary, yet it deeply troubles me that this capability is used to enhance realism rather than gameplay.

When I'm allowed to perform an action in a title that only tells me how incredibly well-programmed it is, instead of said action serving a purpose within the thematic and gameplay loop its title proposes, it's just empty boasting.

Exercising, grocery shopping, refueling, or eating food are impressive in how they're animated and integrated, though none of them truly contribute to the overall gameplay experience that GTA aims to offer; they could disappear, and it would be completely unnoticeable.

Certainly, there's no such thing as necessary or unnecessary in art, so realism for its own sake also has its place. Regardless, I can't help but think that it slows everything down, and as the hours pass, it distracts you, even if only for a few seconds, from the truly captivating things hidden within the state of Leonida.

Like many games, Grand Theft Auto 6 is full of easter eggs for you to discover. These are some of the best Leonida has to offer.

#4178. Why Do I Want To Paint The Walls In Grand Theft Auto VI?

I admire the cozy sim genre. Stardew Valley and Animal Crossing are on regular rotation in my home on my family’s screens, but not my own. In an odd way, I find the genre stressful, arguably the opposite of its intended purpose. I will happily and cathartically guide Grace Ashcroft through the tense hallways of Rhodes Hill in Resident Evil Requiem, but Pokémon Pokopia’s seemingly endless list of to-dos makes me sweat. It’s just not my genre, and I have come to terms with that.

Grand Theft Auto VI is not a cozy game, but it has a substantial amount of cozy elements and mechanics. Bird (and animal) watching, for example, is apparent and encouraged early in the experience. You can also fix up your somewhat dilapidated home from almost the moment you are let loose outside of the opening tutorial missions.

And for some reason, I couldn’t start that process fast enough.

I climbed to the roof to fix the leak and replaced all the stairs leading up to the home before I ever participated in the game’s namesake and stole a car. Normally, it’s the kind of interaction I skip or choose not to engage with, given the option. Or, I do the bare minimum to progress. Sure, I have all the options in the world to build and decorate a house and make it my own, but… that feels like a lot of work. And I am not an artist.

The “cozy” elements of Grand Theft Auto VI are admittedly different from those in a game like Pokopia or Animal Crossing. You’re not designing your home (though you can pick a paint color), but it feels similar, and I am trying to figure out why I enjoy it here as opposed to other games. Is it because Jason and Lucia are so instantly believable as human beings that I want their home to be nicer?

After some thought, I think it might just come down to Grand Theft Auto VI’s consistently impressive visual fidelity. Replacing the shingles on the roof, for example, offers a close-up look at Jason’s character model, and you can practically feel the texture of the asphalt while the heat of the sun beats down.

I don’t have confirmation, but it also just feels like someone at Rockstar did exhaustive research on what the process of replacing a roof shingle should look like, even if, I’m sure, it probably doesn’t quite work that way in the real world. Jason makes it look incredibly easy, to the point that it had me questioning if I should be climbing up to my own roof and taking care of some loose shingles myself. And you know what is a lot of fun? Watching someone who is good at something do the thing they’re good at.

I’m now into the driving and shooting part of the game (and enjoying that, too!), but I am shocked at how grateful I was to have the option to stay home and put up drywall.

#4177. You're not crazy, trying to heal in Nioh 3 sometimes doesn't work - and Team Ninja is fixing it

One of the more insidiously aggravating bugs in Nioh 3 makes it so the game ignores you when you try to use elixirs, but hopefully not for long.

Nioh 3 has received a hot new update that brings plenty of bug fixes to very specific issues, but it also implements fixes for a few of the most common - and incredibly annoying - bugs. Patch 1.03.01 arrived earlier on all platforms, and it comes with a chunky set of notes.

This latest update, predictably, doesn’t add any gameplay features, but some of the included fixes will absolutely delight - or vindicate - so many of the game’s millions of players.

There’s plenty to go through in the patch notes published today for update 1.03.01, but the most impactful is a fix for an issue that “sometimes made it impossible to use elixirs during battle.” This is only a partial fix, but if you ran into the problem of smashing that shortcut button and not seeing your character play the healing animation, you’ll be glad to see it.

This is a problem myself and others have faced, especially in boss fights. You can even see the shortcut register your button press and proceed to ignore you. Another partial fix has been made to an issue that caused the game to crash. Team Ninja didn’t share specifics on that, and though Nioh 3 has been fairly stable for me in 70+ hours, it has definitely crashed a few times.

If you’ve been playing since launch, you likely have - or know someone who has - run into issues with save file corruption and other weird bugs around certain trackable items within save files.

Team Ninja already rolled out a couple of fixes there, and this latest one specifically targets losing valuables during Myths. If your save file has been affected, the game will now check and recover what was lost. Even more interesting is that the game will now automatically create a backup copy of your save data any time you load a save.

If you’ve made it into the Eternal Rift, you’ll be happy to know that today’s update takes care of a few progression blockers, and fixes an issue that allowed some players to obtain certain items before they were supposed to, locking themselves out.

One of the more amusing fixes concerns Mujina, who had a tendency to respawn if you prayed at a Shrine after opening a chest it was hiding in, which made it appear far more often than a mimic should.

Finally, there’s a set of fixes that address bugs (and exploits) when using specific Martial Art with certain weapons. There are a few fixes to AI, Myths, and one problem with the Minamoto no Yoritomo boss fight that made it impossible to interrupt him, even after he runs out of Ki.

Hit the link at the top for the full change log, and check out our Nioh 3 gameplay tips if you haven’t already. You should also change these settings ASAP, as they’re going to make your life much easier and save you a lot of time.

#4176. 4 reasons to play Highway Heroes - Pixel Federation’s relaxing tycoon sim that lets you run trucks across America

Picture yourself cruising down a wide-open road with nothing but your thoughts and your truck with you - if that's possibly the most relaxing thing you can ever imagine, then Highway Heroes might just be your cup of tea.

Pixel Federation's truck tycoon is more than just getting cargo from one spot to another - nor is it all about the stress of keeping a trucking empire afloat. If you still haven't gotten on board with Highway Heroes, here's why you should!

It's essentially a different way of unwinding after a long and hard day, where you can watch your trucks move through a handcrafted map inspired by America in full 3D. It's not just soulless icons that drive here and there - you can marvel at the fruits of your labour as your trucks travel on the road, offering a more meditative experience all throughout. Less about speed, more about strategy That means it's not like other tycoon truck games where speed is of the essence - here, it's really all about smart planning and making sure you strategise every move to keep your business running.

Whether that's figuring out how to handle a certain request depending on your capacity or upgrading your fleet to expand your operations, your decision-making matters more than simply keeping things ticking over. And with your strategies comes the satisfaction of pulling things off in the end too, which adds to the relaxation at the end of the day. Cool customisations for your entire collection More than just a transport game, Highway Heroes is also a truck game, so to speak, so you can expect to spruce up your entire fleet depending on your tastes. As you progress through the levels, you get to unlock more and more cosmetics to help you customise your fleet. Plus, you'll discover rigs and upgrade them to personalise your trucks to your liking.

That's where the beauty of being able to zoom in and out of those 3D truck models comes into play too, by the way - seeing how every detail you've customised reflects onto your fleet certainly adds to the enjoyment of watching your trucks go by. Real-world looks without the real-world stress With idle mechanics thrown into the mix, the transport manager also keeps the real-world stress at bay without compromising on real-world quality. This means that trucks and environments are incredibly detailed, with new regions popping up continuously and themed events keeping things fresh.

The recent Gold Fever, Rocket Runway, and Haul-O-Ween events, for instance, keep the cargo game fresh and continue to immerse players in American trucking culture - as approved by trucking veterans worldwide.

If you're on the hunt for a relaxing yet strategically satisfying truck tycoon sim that respects your time (and taste!), Highway Heroes' realistic trucks and relaxing gameplay might just do the trick.

#4175. Nintendo Promises To Fix The Long Load Times On Pikmin 4 - Switch 2 Edition

Nintendo has issued a statement acknowledging load time issues on Pikmin 4 - Nintendo Switch 2 Edition + Dandori Academy on Switch 2.

The company has promised to released a patch addressing the concerns, citing the long load times that primarily occur when travelling to surface areas. It's also identified an issue in which long loads occur if your network connection is unstable.

While Nintendo works to resolve the issues, it has advised to play in an environment with a stable network connection.

"In Pikmin 4 - Nintendo Switch 2 Edition + Dandori Academy, we have identified an issue where loading times are longer than expected when traveling to surface areas, including the Rescue Camp. We are currently preparing an update to address this. We apologise for any inconvenience this may cause.

"Additionally, we have identified an issue where launching the game or accessing the "Dandori Challenge" (Dandori Test) may take an extended amount of time if the network connection is unstable. We are currently investigating the cause of this issue.

"If you encounter these issues, playing in an environment with a stable network connection may help resolve them."

Pikmin 4 on Switch 2 garnered decent reviews upon release, though it's safe to say that it's not the most beloved update Nintendo has provided for its latest console. Players were immediately put off by the load times, a lack of 60fps, and seemingly slight new content based on existing levels.

Indeed, Nintendo's latest statement has been met with comments from users demanding that 60fps be added to the game, but the company has not acknowledged this, so it seems unlikely to be included at this time.

#4174. GTA 6: Complete Beginner's Guide

Usama Mehmood is a Senior Writer at DualShockers with more than five years of experience in the video game industry. He has been writing professionally since 2021 and covering games since 2022, with work spanning guides, lists, reviews, and features across action-adventure games, JRPGs, open-world titles, racing games,

Pretty sure we’ve all had an eventful week with Grand Theft Auto 6 so far because it is undoubtedly the most ambitious video game release, shattering an entertainment-product record on release and going way beyond people’s expectations with the amount of detail and what it has in store. And undeniably, anyone jumping in for the first time may feel overwhelmed by the mechanics and additions.

Grand Theft Auto 6 delivers an enormous open world, a gripping story, a vibrant Vice City and an astonishing range of activities.

But hey, whether you’re a seasoned veteran of the series or totally new to video games who’s playing this blindly for the first time, you don’t have to worry because I've put together an extensive Beginner’s Guide to GTA 6 that compiles the most helpful tips and explanations of the game’s most complex aspects. Strap in, because this will be worth your time, trust.

I’m getting the formalities out of the way first because I’m quickly going to suggest tuning some settings right from the main menu or even in-game, actually. These are all up to you, but I’m mostly here to show you how each one can be helpful.

First, if you’re used to the OG controls of the GTA series, quickly set the control scheme to Classic, as this brings back some familiar GTA 5-style inputs. By default, running and sprinting are mapped to clicking L3, while jumping is assigned to X (A on Xbox). Switching to Classic moves running and sprinting back to X (A), puts crouching on L3, and swaps a few other actions around. I genuinely find it much more comfortable, especially if you've spent years playing the older games.

Next, I'd recommend setting your Minimap to Always On under UI > Navigation. GTA 6's default Dynamic HUD can hide certain information when you're exploring, which looks great for immersion but isn't always practical when you're still learning your way around Leonida. And while you’re at it, reduce Motion Blur Strength if you don’t want to get sick.

And beyond whichever aiming sensitivity suits you, be sure to experiment with the Targeting settings under Gameplay > Combat. Partial is a good middle ground for newcomers, as it helps move your aim towards nearby targets without completely locking onto them. Finally, in UI > Units of Measurement, you can choose your preferred unit system, like the 12-hour clock over the 24-hour one.

Grand Theft Auto 6 puts a large emphasis on keeping your relationship sound, so you need to know what ways are the best to raise the romance between Jason and Lucia.

Briefly going over this as well, since you can easily handle this, contrary to what other players might have you believe. Jason and Lucia are your own, like the little make-believe babies for a class project. Besides their relationship, keep in mind that these characters now have individual stats, like hunger, muscle mass, weight, and sleep management. These can actively influence gameplay in a few ways, such as sleep affecting your total stamina. Meanwhile, things like weight affect how fast you can sprint.

We already have a list of the best ways to boost the couple’s relationship, but the basic gist that you need to remember is not to let them drop to Partners in Crime or below. There are plenty of things that can help you easily boost their relationship, so it’s honestly impossible to not maintain it unless you’re purposely not using both characters or sabotaging it yourself.

And since we’re here, make sure to actively invest in the couple’s BuckMe Family Savings account later on until you max it out at the highest tier, since both that and their relationship are among the primary factors influencing the ending of GTA 6.

Again, you’re free to check our dedicated guide on the mechanic as well, but with the Criminal Profile system, just think of it as a more approachable karma system, like the Honor one from Red Dead 2. This is also one of the other parameters that can influence GTA 6’s ending. A lot of people will have you believe that it strips away your maniacal “GTA” playstyle, but trust me, with everything in your power, this is the most forgiving and manipulable mechanic in the game.

The only thing to watch out for is taking things to the “Irredeemable” state because by that point you can’t revert it back, and you’ll be stuck with that profile unless you have a save file. You can achieve and maintain a Professional Criminal Profile by simply being a good citizen or trying to have as few casualties as possible during side activities, or even successfully making clean getaways and stealth takedowns.

Don’t be afraid to take headshots when necessary because even if you reach a state like Psycho, you can easily change that back by petting a couple of domestic animals, spending some casual time with each other, or just by avoiding headshots altogether for the next few kills by shooting in the limbs instead.

GTA 6 has a noticeably more complex Wanted System than its predecessors. For starters, we’re back to six Wanted Stars, and the police are now much more observant of our actions. Witnesses can report your crimes, security cameras can capture your current identity, and even certain high-end vehicles have trackers that forbid you from just stealing them. In other words, no more crazy Grand Theft Auto-ing.

The biggest change, however, is the introduction of the Heat system. Even after you've managed to lose the cops, they will still remember certain identifying details about you, including your appearance, clothing, getaway vehicle, visible weapons, and whether Jason and Lucia were together. These are represented by small red icons underneath your Wanted Stars, so pay attention to them whenever you're trying to escape.

It’s either how fast you can clear the heat markers off of you in the natural way or some creative tactics that I can suggest, like using water vehicles or boats for escaping higher-level wanted stars, since the rivers and sea tend to be open and less swamped with traffic than VC’s urban infrastructure.

Money plays a much bigger role in GTA 6 than you might initially expect, and you'll quickly find yourself needing extra cash to purchase weapons, clothing for both characters, vehicle upgrades, and other necessities. Thankfully, Leonida is practically overflowing with opportunities to make a quick buck. But the progression works steadily throughout each chapter here.

You’ll start off small by robbing convenience stores and other local businesses in chapter 2, but by chapters 3 and 4, the Robberies tab on your map will be almost flooded with bigger opportunities, including pawn shops, jewelry stores, and banks. Even the occasional gang hideout has different valuables like unique guns to own, vehicles to sell, or safes to bust open and loot.

However, be mindful that robbing a place blind isn't always the smartest idea since many of these sites have security cameras and alarms. Try to use Focus Mode as much as possible to identify enemies, valuable items, and locate safe combinations before making your escape.

Of course, not everything in Leonida requires you to point a gun at someone. There are several side activities that can help you earn some extra money, including stealing vehicles for buyers like Moses and Randy, hunting wildlife for Bret, and competing in Demolition Derbies at Ambrosia Raceway.

One final thing worth remembering is that GTA 6 has three forms of allowance: pocket cash, bank savings, and the valuables you carry in your stash bag. While your bank balance is safe, getting Wasted or Busted can cost you the cash you're carrying, along with any stolen goods you haven't managed to sell, so make a habit of visiting ATMs to deposit your earnings into BuckMe whenever possible.

Many of us are already feeling nostalgic about GTA 6’s first chapter; I mean, seriously, the vibe in Key Lento is unparalleled, especially when playing the game for the first time. But as all things come and go, the vibe doesn't last for long here.

There are a handful of missables you can easily overlook if you rush through the story, so I'd strongly recommend taking your time and exploring everything the Keys have to offer before moving on. Without spoiling, The Tourist Trap mission marks the point of no return for Chapter 1's free roam, so make sure you’re fully ready.

For starters, make sure you complete Shirley's optional jobs, Get Shirley's Rum and Steal the Scooter, as these are exclusive to the first chapter. You might also want to check the loose floorboards for any money you've stashed away, and deposit that into your BuckMe Family Savings.

Lastly, it doesn’t hurt to have a separate manual save for this chapter specifically since GTA 6 doesn't currently let you replay completed story missions, so having a backup gives you the opportunity to revisit Key Lento without having to start another playthrough.

You don't necessarily need to complete every single activity before moving on, but I'd hate for you to miss out on some of the more interesting encounters and neat discoveries Rockstar’s tucked away in this opening chapter. Trust me, you'll appreciate this thing the most here.

Grand Theft Auto 6 makes you lose everything at the end of the first chapter, so make sure that you complete these necessary tasks before taking the plunge into chapter two.

#4173. Grand Theft Auto VI's Auto Drive Is A Beautiful And Free Version Of Hands-Free Travel

Grand Theft Auto VI is a game where you spend a lot of time behind the wheel. Always has been. But sometimes, you just won't feel like actively driving, but you also don't to waste money on a cab.

This is where Auto Drive comes in. It lets the game take over and drive you where you need to go in real time and all with a cinematic camera that shifts and moves, letting you take in the environment without all that pesky "having to pay attention to the road." Red Dead Redemption 2 had the same feature, and I have fond memories of taking advantage of it to watch Arthur ride his horse through that game's incredible environment. It's a great option in GTAVI, but how to use it and turn it on isn't immediately apparent.

First, you must select a destination. Get the GPS set up to direct you to where you want to go.

Next, start driving. The Auto Drive is smart, but doesn't seem to be smart enough to make three-point turns or back out of parking lots. You need to be on your way before you can turn it on.

Once you're on the path, hold down in the d-pad and press start to activate Cinematic.

Once you've done this you should be able to hold down the Circle button on PlayStation or the B button on Xbox to activate Auto Drive and... voilà! You can sit back and let Jason or Lucia take the wheel. They will drive legally, even stopping at lights, but you can speed them up if they're taking too long.

I've always enjoyed driving in Grand Theft Auto, but I was grateful to find this almost-hidden option early in the game.

Krafton has a new music project on the go called The Squad, and K-pop group IVE is the first act involved. It spans both PUBG: Battlegrounds and PUBG Mobile, so this time those of you on iOS and Android get in on it as well, with collab content heading to mobile in December.

IVE was already in Battlegrounds earlier this month. That was the Love Dive collab, which brought themed content to Rondo along with some character items and cosmetics, and it was a fairly soft, pretty sort of affair.

Going forward, Krafton wants a run of different artists to each make an original song inspired by PUBG, and every one of them gets their own themed stuff in the games off the back of it. More are on the way after IVE, apparently, which ties in with PUBG's tenth anniversary coming up in 2027.

As for when it all lands, PC is first on December 2nd and PUBG Mobile gets it on December 7th, then console on the 10th. PC and console get themed locations to drop into too. Mobile isn't mentioned for those, so it's items only for now, as far as I can see.

#4170. Genshin Impact Luna 5 takes the squad back to Mondstadt, finally makes Varka playable

Genshin Impact's next update will have you reminiscing about the good ol' days of... 2020.

The latest big content update has been revealed for HoYoverse's breakout game, Genshin Impact. Version Luna 5, which has the unusually long and needlessly layered title — Song of the Welkin Moon: Variation - Homeward, He Who Caught the Wind — is set to arrive February 25.

This one is a bit of a nostalgia play, taking everyone back to Mondstadt, the place where you may remember taking your first steps. And, as with any good return to the ol’ hunting grounds, come familiar characters, too.

The big new arrival is Varka, who joins as a playable character for the first time. Varka, Grand Master of the Knights of Favonius, is a character whose debut has been long-awaited. He is a 5-Star Anemo Claymore wielder with a dual-wield combat style, capable of dealing two different types of Elemental damage. His addition means that there's now finally a burly 5-Star male character of each elemental type... do with that information what you will.

Varka's dual-wielding combat style allows him to deal two different types of Elemental damage at the same time. The way it works is that his Elemental Skill boosts the damage of his regular attacks, but it also converts the damage type of his right-hand claymore to match his teammates’ elements (Pyro, Hydro, Electro, or Cryo). The left-hand claymore always deals Anemo damage.

The more normal attacks you use, the more frequently he can activate a special Elemental Skill, or trigger a Charged Attack that doesn’t consume stamina. He can also rely on the Hexerei effect to trigger more instances of Elemental Skill, as well as Charged Attacks, making him a monster damage-dealer.

Varka, of course, has been a staple member of the cast, featuring in both the original story in a small cameo, as well as taking a bigger role in the recent Nod-Krai chapters. With the return to Mondstadt, his playable debut makes sense. His Story Quest will shed light on his encounter with the Wild Hunt, and the Great Wolf King of the North

The reruns for this version are going to be Flins — who will be available in the first phase of Event Wishes — as well as Skirk and Escoffier in the second phase. You can also look forward to the return of the Chronicled Wish with Mondstadt characters.

Staying on the theme of reminiscence, the big event in Luna 5 is centered around revisiting memories from the beginning of your time with Genshin Impact, and reuniting with old friends. In Echoes of Memory, you’ll witness familiar scenes that have been changed slightly, and you’ll need to use the Spotter Kamera to detect and record those differences.

The Knights of Favonius are hosting several other activities for everyone to take part in, including an event that lets you catch up with old friends over drinks which you make for them.

Outside of events, there’s a new set of Gliding and Combat Challenges. And, of course, there are new minigames that you can relax with. The Kamera is being utilised yet again, and this time you can use to capture sights from your time in spots across Natlan, Fontaine, and Sumeru. There’s also… a horde mode of a sort, where you fend off waves of enemies.

Tales of streakers were some of the first leaks to breach GTA 6, and those on the hunt may be a bit disappointed.

Hidden within the humble little town of Hamlet is a wrestling legend ready to take on all challengers, while putting his own pride on the line. If you’re up to snuff and want to become the next Backyard Wrestling Champion, read on to claim your spoils.

In order to find the Champ, you’ll need to head back to Hamlet once you regain control of Jason in Chapter 2. Head to the street between the grocery store and the gas station towards the middle of town. Look for the backyard of one of the houses containing a ring, a trailer, and a big Backyard Wrestling banner.

Knock on the door of the trailer to get some dialogue from the Champ, where he’ll refuse to come out. Toss a nearby can or bottle, then knock again for him to make his entrance, toss Jason to the ground, and drag him into the ring for a little one-on-one playtime. If you can last against the Gentrifier, you’ll be the new Champ.

Once he’s introduced himself, the Gentrifier will put Jason into a series of grapple-based Quick Time Events. Make sure you boost your Stamina with a drink or snack of some kind before you get started to ensure you’ve got as much time to mash as possible.

Once you clear two of these mash-fests, the Gentrifier will toss Jason to the ground before going for his finishing move, the Eviction Notice. React with Square on PS5/X on XBOX to dive out of the wave, leaving him open for a counter. Don’t waste your time stomping on him. Instead, climb the same post he tried to use, and end it with a soaring People’s Elbow.

Once he’s down and out, you can ransack his trailer for some cash, some drugs, his own stylin’ shades, and a one-of-one Luchador mask that can serve as a disguise for either character. A fantastic little token of a victory hard-fought, cementing Jason as the Backyard Wrestling Champion.

Last year's wonderful roguelike, Absolum, is the next game in the spotlight, available for free to all those with a Nintendo Switch Online subscription in Europe from tomorrow (27th November) until 3rd December.

"It’s incredibly impressive in its reconstitution of arcade, role-playing, and roguelike formats, evolving them into something fresh and exciting," we said in our 9/10 review, describing it as "one of the best of its kind, whatever that kind may be".

In short, a chance to check it out for free is a welcome one.

#4166. Digging Deep 2 offers Motherload-style mining and exploration, out now on Android

As I often say, you can trace a direct line from the world of Flash games to the popular picks on mobile today. Just take a look at Digging Deep, and you can see more than a bit of inspiration from the classic Motherload. But in Digging Deep 2: Mine & Build, developer Bitrealms Studio is going even bigger than before.

Digging Deep 2's aim is simple: you have a base and a mining rig. You need to mine downwards into the shaft, navigating across each node and seeking out both ore to take back to the surface, as well as oxygen to let you dig deeper. Not to mention keeping your sensors peeled for crew members still trapped below.

It's all quite simple, but not primitive. If, like me, you sank hours into Motherload, then you can definitely see the appeal. And it's a formula other developers have run with, including the likes of Dome Keeper, which took a more minimalist approach to the format.

Finally, if you want even more challenge, you can unlock the Volcano and see how long you last in its metal-melting depths. All in all, if you're looking for mining and exploration, Digging Deep 2 looks to be a neat little option.

Speaking of new releases though, maybe you're in the mood for something a little more introspective? Well, in that case you're in luck, because I've just reviewed Vampire Therapist, an engaging and intriguing visual novel that has you working to help your fellow undead to cope with their immortal problems.

#4164. Nioh 3 is, unsurprisingly, the fastest-selling game in the series with over a million units sold

Nioh 3 has taken the Nioh franchise to new heights, delivering its biggest-ever launch.

Even before the game came out, it was pretty easy to guess that Nioh 3 would be a hit. From the word of mouth leading up to launch, to the well-received free demo, there was little chance the action RPG wasn’t going to be a major deal.

Today, publisher Koei Tecmo has announced that the game has officially passed over one million copies sold worldwide across PC, and PlayStation 5. This makes it the fastest in the Nioh franchise to reach this milestone.

As a result of this fantastic launch, Nioh 3 has now pushed overall Nioh franchise sales to be over 10 million, which includes the original Nioh as well as Nioh 2. Today’s news comes just two weeks after the game arrived on PC, and PS5.

On Steam, where it’s available on PC, it shot up the Steam charts, and immediately broke the series’ previous best peak concurrent player count record. From there, the numbers kept growing, leading up to a stellar weekend where it peaked at 88,045 concurrent players on Steam, double that of its launch day.

This now stands as the largest for any Nioh game on Steam, and though we don’t have insight into how well it’s doing on PS5 specifically, it still shows that the Nioh series continues to grow.

Nioh 3 builds on everything the two prior games established, and pushes the series into the semi-open-world realm, with several larger maps that each cover a period of time in Japan’s history. In our Nioh 3 review we called it “Team Ninja’s most accomplished action game, and the series’ most accessible.”

If you’re curious about the challenging and very rewarding action RPG, start with these gameplay tips, and don’t be shy to call upon a friend (or stranger) for help using our co-op guide.

#4163. Blackwater Mill is an ambitious, if flawed, horror game from a small Yorkshire studio

It seems as though every facet of American society has been explored in horror, from the high towers of luxury to the dark backwoods. But the same is not true of other countries, including the UK, especially with so many dark, decrepit corners to explore. That's what Yorkshire bashed Wrenhaven Ltd. are looking to resolve with their upcoming mobile horror game Blackwater Mill.

Blackwater Mill sees you step into the role of Sam, the project manager for the demolition of the titular mill. Venturing up into the Pennine mountains of Yorkshire during a dark, rainy night, you find yourself trapped in the mill, and it's up to you to find out what happened to leave it infested with the unquiet dead.

Miller lite Now let's address the elephant in the room, or the mine at least. Blackwater Mill is not a particularly good-looking game; in fact, you might say it looks positively crude. But, equally, I can't help but admire the ambition Wrenhaven Ltd. has put into this. A five-chapter horror game is ambitious even for full studios, let alone a tiny indie.

And, in truth, there's not much in the way of Brit horror on other platforms, let alone on mobile. If you've never had the pleasure of visiting abandoned mines on a tour, and feeling the all-pervading darkness when the lights go out, it's hard to describe how mesmerising and terrifying it can be.

To be honest, if you can get past the initial (very) janky graphics, there's something also rather unnerving about Blackwater Mill's undead miners. And while it may not sway those of you who want a high-fidelity experience on mobile, it's well worth a look when it does release for Android very soon, and iOS later.

In the meantime, if you want to see what other spine-chillers there are on mobile, why not take a look at our list of the best horror games on Android? Featuring plenty of bona fide terrors to keep you up these long winter nights.

#4162. Team Cherry Unveils New Original Titles, Sea of Sorrow Release Date

Patrick Souza is a writer for DualShockers who has been writing for over 5 years, specializing in JRPGs, roguelikes, and other genres such as MMOs. He previously worked for Prima Games, The Escapist, and The Gamer, and holds a degree in Journalism.

Team Cherry has done it once again with its eccentric reveals, as its latest livestream presentation Cherry Time has revealed not only the release date for the upcoming DLC for Hollow Knight: Silksong, but also some brand-new original titles.

Previously known mostly for the original Hollow Knight, the studio is now expanding its catalogue to actually include some more indie titles from different genres, but not without giving some love to the original game that first made them famous.

These are long awaited video game sequels that met the hype and lived up to our expectations.

Sea of Sorrow, a free expansion adding tons of new areas, bosses, challenges, quality-of-life improvements, and some new lore pieces for Silksong, is described as an “expansion like they never did before” and will be dropping on December 11, free for all players.

The Cherry Time livestream has revealed the latest trailer for the Silksong expansion, complete with its release date and a small tease for its bosses. Just like with the base game, the release date was revealed exactly two weeks before its launch.

First announced earlier this week, the stream was a welcome surprise for the fans, filled with new footage from the new areas Hornet will visit and small showcases of what we can expect in this new adventure. And if we can take the original Hollow Knight expansions as a baseline, we’re in for a huge treat here.

We can see new scenes of Hornet running across the new areas and the new enemies she’ll be facing in these distant waters. A favorite of mine is the new pirate-like boss, which is one of the main focuses in this trailer. We can also see some platforming sessions and at least one new of the dreaded enemy gauntlets in the trailer, so get ready to put those tools to use.

And speaking of tools, the biggest highlight obviously goes to the final scene, where Hornet actually unveils a new tool being used for the most ancient practice in any good RPG: fishing. Love it or hate it, the game wouldn’t be complete without it, and you know it. And in classic Hollow Knight fashion, expect some obscure secret to be hidden beneath the fishing waters.

For now, I’m hoping for more challenging areas such as the Cogwork Core and fewer areas that are just a torture session in a trench coat, such as Bilewater.

Aside from Sea of Sorrow news, Team Cherry also promised more “exciting announcements”, and they did deliver. Previously known as the studio that wouldn’t speak with its public while working on their game (in a very justified way), this now seems to be in the past as the small South Australian studio came forward not only with a release date for the expansion, but also with brand-new titles developed by the studio.

These include Blokan: Secret of the Walking City, a new game by Hollow Knight artist Rohan Fraser. It follows a detective solving cases in a traditional puzzle game style above a fantasy-inspired city, fully drawn by hand. It is inspired by the traditional golden age adventure games, according to Fraser himself.

Radio Rain is another one, a side-scrolling title made by Lukas Stobie, who previously developed Rising Dusk. This new side-scrolling adventure game follows the protagonist as she finds her way across the ruins of a rainy world filled with music, all in an amazing pixel art style.

The final reveal is The Botanist and The Translator, developed by Makoto Kuji (the voice of Hornet herself). In this 2d adventure game, you’ll play as the botanist-investigator Hatti and her animal translator partner Oliver, who work together to unveil a mystery while exploring a beautifully hand-drawn Sailor Moon-inspired world.

It’s amazing to see Team Cherry actually growing up as a studio, as they can now reliably deliver more titles and not be bound to the same franchise for years. While the Hollow Knight games might still be their magnum opus, knowing that we’ll see more of its DNA implemented across different titles is an even better gift than I could’ve asked for. Especially now that Sea of Sorrow is coming.

This list covers the most important things to complete in Hollow Knight: Silksong before moving on to the Sea of Sorrow DLC.

#4161. The Video Games You Should Play This Weekend – November 20, 2026

This is it. We finally made it. Grand Theft Auto VI is here. I have played the game for a number of hours and read Matt Miller's glowing review, which you can read here, and I still don't know if I personally believe the game is actually out. But that just might the lack of sleep from staying up late to play Grand Theft Auto VI.

Many games chose to avoid the blast radius of Rockstar's latest crime caper, but that doesn't mean it's the only game that came out this week and you can find them below. But as is tradition, here are some of our top stories of the week first.

If you’re not aware that GTAVI launched this week, it’s possible that you’ve been living under a rock somewhere. Nonetheless, we’re here to offer the reminder that after more than a decade of waiting for a new installment, Rockstar has this week rolled out its new game. It’s good. Like, really good, and if you’re an adult who plays video games, it should really be a title you make time for.

In my review, I highlighted some of its many positive traits, but as you prepare to dive into its criminal delights over the weekend, one element I’d especially like to point out is its viability as a game to play with your partner. Like an excellent prestige TV crime show, GTAVI is a game that features a rich, dramatic, funny, and well-written story that I genuinely believe has the potential to be a good time for both a player and a viewer, though, admittedly, the person who gets to enjoy running the sticks is probably having the most fun.

However you plan to enjoy it, here’s hoping Grand Theft Auto VI turns out to be worth the wait you’ve likely had for it. For my part, it certainly has been, and I suspect you’ll find it only gets better the deeper into the game you go.

The running joke publisher Devolver Digital has made with this “spectacular remaster of the original remake of the unreleased action-platformer starring the most famous video game mascot of all time” is that it launched the same day as Grand Theft Auto VI. Volvy’s Adventure has been positioned as a tongue-in-cheek competitor to Rockstar’s behemoth, with Devovler even releasing a trailer that is a shot-for-shot parody of GTA VI’s. While I’ve chuckled at these stunts, Volvy’s Adventure isn’t just a joke game. It’s actually pretty fun.

For one, it’s developed by a respectable studio in Doinksoft, the team behind fun indie games like Gato Roboto, Gunbrella, and this year’s Dark Scrolls. Vovly’s Adventure is a 16-bit 2D platformer where players use Volvy’s oversized fist to punch through objects, which, in turn, propels him in the same direction. Thus, platforming is a fast-paced and explosive exercise in soaring fist-first through barriers and enemies, collecting items, and burrowing through certain platforms. The platforming feels pretty good, and it’s backed by a catchy soundtrack; the destruction is satisfying; and the levels are relatively brief, making it easy to plow through.

I wasn’t sure what to expect from Volvy’s Adventure beyond the marketing jokes, but it’s got some sauce. Sitting at the budget price of $5 (and a launch discount of $3.74), it’s a curiosity that’s easy to check out.

Australia Did It, from Rami Ismail and his team at Aesthetician Labs, hit a little snag with its publicized release date. Valve got backed up approving the release of games on its platform and a handful of games were affected. Australia Did It, despite the unexpected delay, is out... and it's good! Here's what Brian Shea wrote in his review: "Looking back on the hours I poured into Australia Did It, the forgettable train segments will occupy only a small part of my memories, just as they do in each run. Instead, what will stick with me for months to come are the creative combination mechanics, the outstanding turn-based defense system, and the thrill of uncovering the mysteries of this bleak, yet engaging world."

God of War Sons of Sparta is... underwhelming, to be blunt. You can read my review here. The game is a prequel where you play as a young Kratos and go on a 2D Metroid-inspired adventure with your brother, Deimos. If you are interested in getting the full God of War story, there are some interesting narrative and character details in the game, but it has some shortcomings. What's surprising about its re-release this week is that it is now available on PS4. An unexpected "new" platform to say the least.

#4159. Knight & Dragon Side Story turns the text-based JRPG from turn-based to real-time

We cover a lot of smaller, more niche series on the site here. And one of them that has recently cropped up is Knight & Dragon, a text-based JRPG series full of plenty of number-crunching and grind. Now, developer Shinjiro Nakagawa is trying something new with the launch of Knight & Dragon Side Story.

As you may have already gleaned from the headline, the core change of Knight & Dragon Side Story is that it ditches the traditional turn-based JRPG combat in favour of real-time action. It's not fully 3D, however, as instead you'll be tasked with actively dodging attacks in the style of something like Undertale, making for a more fast-paced adventure.

For me, the only issue is the traces of AI art seen in some of the icons, at least to my eye. Which is a shame because I think part of the charm of the Knight & Dragon series is the way in which they work by using text and basic icons. You lose some of that with the generated assets.

Still, if you're willing to give it a shot, I reckon that this will present a very interesting departure from the norm for fans of Knight & Dragon. And you can find it right now on iOS and Android!

In the meantime, though, if you want, you can find some of the other big releases on mobile that we think are worth playing in one simple place. Our list of the five new mobile games to try this week offers some interesting picks which we think are worth checking out.

Download now! Knight & Dragon Side Story

#4158. The Sims 4 developer hasn't forgotten about its quality of life commitment, and is back with an update on what to expect in 2026

Maxis has offered some fresh details on its long-running mission to improve player quality of life in The Sims 4.

As the The Sims 4 continues into its second decade, the volume of new content, major expansions, and long-awaited features has grown in lockstep. Unfortunately, that has also meant that, given how old the game is, a few technical problems remain a nuisance.

The effort required to fix them is what led developer Maxis to make a commitment to improve the game’s technical state, and the developer has now returned to update the community on what to expect in 2026.

The quality of life pledge was made in September last year, through the introduction of a roadmap. Since then, the developer issued one update on its progress. Which brings us to this week’s new blog post, which further builds on everything that’s come before.

In the post, Maxis revealed a few key areas it’s going to be focusing on going forward. Though specific release dates for these changes were not shared, the list of issues should resonate with many players, as it covers many often-discussed topics.

The first stage of the new roadmap covers March through August. Over that period, you can expect Sims' autonomy to improve. This goes for things like how they choose locations for certain actions, they way they interact with certain objects, and even how often they interrupt conversations.

The infant and caregiver relationship is being updated, too, in order to improve autonomy and make sure your little Sims don’t miss out on milestones and interactions. That stage of the roadmap also includes fixes for black photo issues, and other crashes and freezing.

The next period takes place September through December, and it includes more interesting changes. One of the goals with this one is to improve Sims’ dining experience, which covers issues around eating and drinking.

Another important area of focus with this stage is family trees, and relationships between members of the same family. Maxis wants to improve the game’s genealogy systems to make relationship tracking across generations more robust so that your family history isn’t lost.

Depending on how the first stage goes, you might see more issues join the list of what the developer is looking at for the second stage of the roadmap.

The good news is that you won’t have to wait too long for the game’s next patch. Due out in March, this next update will feature around 55 fixes, including for some commonly reported issues.

Until then, you may want to check out The Sims 4’s Lost Legacies Event, which is available now until the middle of March. If you picked up the game’s latest expansion, check if you tried those Royalty & Legacy cheats.
